Borthwick is a gigantic righty who drives way down the mound and misses bats with a plus slider. His build and delivery are very similar to Alek Manoah's, except Borthwick isn't quite that big yet. His slider falls off the table and he locates it well, just off the corner of the plate. It will be important for him to develop a third pitch in pro ball. His build, lack of current repertoire depth, and the effort in his delivery combine to create a good bit of relief risk here.

Borthwick entered the summer showcase circuit as a very large -- he’s 6-foot-6 and listed at 255 pounds -- and intriguing two-way high school player from the Florida panhandle. He showed off skills at the plate, hitting .300 for Team USA at the WSBC U-18 World Cup in Japan, but he really took off with his work on the mound. After pitching well at events like the East Coast Pro Showcase and tossing 10 shutout innings for Team USA, earning tournament MVP honors, it’s clear that his future as a pro will be as a right-handed hurler. Borthwick has the size, pitch mix and makeup to be a future workhorse starter near the top of a big league rotation one day. While he’ll sit 93-95 mph mostly with his fastball, he’s shown the ability to get the heater up to 97-98 mph with good life up in the zone and to both sides of the plate. His best secondary offering is a hard 84-85 mph slider that can flash plus and miss a ton of bats. He has a really good feel for spin, though at times he can try to do too much. There’s some feel for a changeup with some fading action, but he doesn’t use it much. While Borthwick can get a little east-west with his delivery, something very correctable, he shows the ability to pitch to all four quadrants effectively. He’s a power-hitting corner infielder who could get the chance to do both should he go on to Auburn, but he profiles as the kind of high-ceiling arm that goes early enough to forego heading to campus.

Rose is a former catcher who has become a contact-oriented corner outfielder in college. Advanced bat control drives an offensive skill set that it diluted by Rose's tendency to chase. He could be a Harold Ramírez type of role player as a part-time corner outfielder.

A veteran of Major League Baseball’s Dream Series, Rose started making a bigger name for himself on the Draft scene with solid performances at summer showcase events like the PDP League. The Chicago native moved to Florida to attend IMG Academy for his senior year to get a bigger challenge and more exposure, and he continued to show off some exciting tools, even if evaluators aren’t exactly sure where he’ll play at the next level. Rose has the chance to be an impact hitter in the future. He has excellent bat speed and plus raw power, especially to his pull side, though he doesn’t have the most natural swing -- a mechanical tweak that can be made at the next level. He has plus straight run speed and projects to be at least an above-average runner on the basepaths. Some of that projection is impacted by where he plays long-term defensively. Rose is agile behind the plate and some believe he could develop into a solid backstop, something he’s eager to prove, though he would invariably slow down. Others feel the Louisville recruit has too far to go as a catcher and his speed/athleticism would look better in center field. Wherever he plays, his leadership skills and makeup will be huge plusses for any organization that drafts him.

Ruiz is one of the better high school shortstop defenders of the last several years and projects as a plus-plus glove at the position. He's also a smaller athlete who will be 19 on draft day. With the cement relatively dry on his 5-foot-10 frame, he is unlikely to grow into meaningful power and is more likely to be a second-division regular or excellent utilityman.

In 2024, The Stony Brook School from Long Island, New York, won the 2024 NYSAIS State Championship. In 2025, the school held its own by going 2-2 at USA Baseball's National High School Invitational. At the center of it all for the Bears was Ruiz, their shortstop, who then went on to perform at summer events like the East Coast Professional Showcase and Area Code Games. He also manned shortstop for Team USA, moving fellow Draft prospect Grady Emerson to third, and was named to the All-World team as the U.S. brought home gold in the WBSC U-18 World Cup. An undersized switch-hitter who is listed at 5-foot-10 and 168 pounds, Ruiz is arguably the best defensive shortstop in the class. He's an elite defender with a plus arm and range, great hands and outstanding footwork. Unlike with many young players at the premium position, Ruiz not only makes the spectacular, acrobatic plays, throwing on the run, he also slows the game down and makes the routine plays as well. It's future Gold Glove-caliber defense. An above-average runner whose instincts help him be a successful base-stealer, Ruiz's bat is behind his glove. He makes a ton of contact with an idea of what he's doing at the plate, excellent bat control and no fear, showing an ability to turn around premium velocity. But he's done it without too much damage or impact to date, and showing some ability to drive the ball could certainly help the Vanderbilt recruit's Draft stock.

Wisener has one of the better breaking balls among the high school pitchers in the 2026 class, a two-planed sweeper in the 81-86 mph range. Wisener was sitting 94-96 for one inning at Area Codes in 2025 and then was sitting there again at the start of 2026. His fastball runs downhill and is going to play down unless he leans into sink. Wisener is usually very balanced and under control as he lands and finishes his delivery, which helps him locate the baseball consistently. Sharp command might help his breaking ball play like a premium weapon. He's an older seven-figure prospect.

Teel hit .321/.442/.577 in two years at Virginia and was a draft-eligible sophomore in 2025 who transferred to Mississippi State for 2026 rather than humor the draft process. He doesn't have huge top-end speed but did some incredible stuff on defense toward the end of the 2025 season, diving in the gaps with no regard for his own well being. Teel could be passable in center on grit and instincts, but is more likely to rove all over the outfield. He posted a 95% zone contact rate in 2025. Teel swings bent at the waist, which helps facilitate excellent plate coverage. Style can look slash-and-dash-y on the surface, but Teel has consistent feel for elevation. Makes well-struck contact to all fields. Would be a doubles machine if he had half a grade more power. Well-rounded fourth outfield prospect.

A physical, mistake-crushing second baseman, Rembert slashed .344/.467/.555 with more walks than strikeouts during his freshman season at Auburn and .370/.414/.648 combined between Cape Cod and Team USA activity during the summer. He's a draft-eligible sophomore in 2026. Rembert's power is his best tool. He's a short-levered hitter but strong enough to have hit some big pull-side blasts in 2025, and though his swing is fairly flat, he seems to have feel for impacting the bottom of the baseball and generating loft. An outsized portion of his contact is both hard and in the air; his barrel rate was a little more than two standard deviations above he NCAA average last year. Because Rembert is a second base-only defender, he needs to get to that power in games as a pro. Some of his underlying data (his in-zone contact rate was a little worse than the NCAA average, more starkly after conference play began) suggests that his hit tool might not be able to sustain the 14% K% he managed in 2025. He's an early second round prospect.

Scouts appreciated Rembert's bat when he was a Florida high school senior in 2024 but weren't sure about the rest of his game and didn't try to deter him from attending Auburn. After earning consensus Freshman All-America honors and posting the best batting average (.278 in five games) on the U.S. collegiate national team last year, he's poised to become one of the first sophomore-eligibles selected in 2026. He has proven that he can handle second base at the next level and earns comparisons to Howie Kendrick and Christian Moore. Rembert has some of the best bat speed in college baseball and an advanced approach, though his swing and patience have regressed a bit this spring. He manages the strike zone very well and focuses on drilling line drives from gap to gap. It's unclear if he'll provide more than 15 homers annually because he makes too much groundball contact, though he has the strength and bat speed to do more damage if he turns on more pitches and adds more loft to his compact right-handed stroke. Rembert is an average runner with arm strength to match, which limits his usefulness on the bases and in the field. Some scouts once wondered if he'd wind up in left field, but he's looking more comfortable at second base in college than he did at shortstop in high school. He has reliable hands and provides steady defense at the keystone.

Brick reclassified from the 2027 group after he hit well with Team USA at the U19 World Cup in Japan. Though we have more limited and less reliable showcase data for Brick because he was facing a lot of 2027s during the last two years, the data we do have is very positive; an 83% contact rate on a projectable 6-foot-2 catcher. Brick moves the barrel around the zone well and his top hand drives his swing, giving him a shot to grow into a blend of contact and power. Brick has a ton of developing to do on defense. His crouch is high, and his footwork is erratic. Those don't add risk to his profile so much as they'll likely add time to his developmental journey.

Christian Brothers HS (Memphis, Tenn.) has sent 11 players to the Majors, most notably All-Star catcher Tim McCarver. The Purple Wave now have the best prep catching prospect in the 2026 Draft after Brick reclassified from the 2027 class. He made that decision in October after starring for Team USA at the 18-and-under World Cup in Japan, batting .333 while providing quality defense behind the plate as the second-youngest player on the squad. Brick's best tool is his well-above-average arm strength, as he regularly records sub-1.9-second pop times and can throw out basestealers from his knees. He moves well behind the plate and shows the potential to become a solid receiver and blocker once he improves his one-knee technique. He didn't have any issues handling the premium stuff he saw with the U.S. 18-and-under team and scouts rave about his makeup. Brick's bat hasn't been as good as anticipated this spring. The Mississippi State recruit has a quick right-handed stroke but gets too passive at times and his long levers result in some in-zone swing-and-miss worries. He displays plus raw power in batting practice but focuses more on hitting line drives during game action.

Brick's best tool is his well-above-average arm strength, as he regularly records sub-1.9-second pop times and can throw out basestealers from his knees. He moves well behind the plate and shows the potential to become a solid receiver and blocker once he improves his one-knee technique. He didn't have any issues handling the premium stuff he saw with the U.S. 18-and-under team and scouts rave about his makeup. Brick's bat hasn't been as good as anticipated this spring. The Mississippi State recruit has a quick right-handed stroke but gets too passive at times and his long levers result in some in-zone swing-and-miss worries. He displays plus raw power in batting practice but focuses more on hitting line drives during game action.

Maniscalco is a very athletic young shortstop who was originally going to be part of the 2027 class, but reclassified to 2026. He'll be just a shade over 17 years old on draft day. Maniscalco is a switch-hitter with a sweet lefty swing and acrobatic actions on defense. He's very skinny, but he's also 17. He's got a chance to go very high in the draft depending on how his body develops between now and the summer. If he has become meaningfully stronger, he could be this draft's Jordan Yost or Steele Hall.

When scouts went to see 2024 Marlins second-rounder Carter Johnson at Oxford (Ala.) HS, they couldn't help but notice Maniscalco, then a freshman. He has reclassified into the 2026 Draft and will be one of the youngest players (17 years, two months) selected in years. He shares some similarities to Eli Willits, who reclassified into the 2025 Draft and went No. 1 overall, with Maniscalco possessing more power potential but less speed. The biggest difference is that Willits starred in his final high school season while Maniscalco looked overmatched at the plate during his before rallying some later in the spring. While Maniscalco had a reputation for having a very advanced approach for his age, he has looked too aggressive at times and too passive at others while struggling to make contact against Alabama high school pitching. Evaluators are willing to cut him some slack because of his youth, but they don't like the deep trigger in his swing. A switch-hitter, he has a markedly better stroke from the left side. Though there now are concerns about his hitting ability, most scouts believe he'll develop average or better power once he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame. Maniscalco is presently an average runner, with some scouts wondering if he might get a bit quicker as he adds strength and others speculating that he might lose a step. There's no question about the Mississippi State recruit's ability to remain at shortstop, where he has smooth actions and projects as a plus defender with arm strength to match. The son of Matt Maniscalco, who made it to Triple-A as a shortstop in the Rays system and runs his travel ball program, Rocco has developed a high baseball IQ while growing up around the game.

Comeau is a very projectable 6-foot-4 lefty-hitting infielder whose slower twitch actions will likely make him a better long-term fit at third base. He showed good plate coverage during his showcase summer, especially for one of the younger, longer-levered hitters in the class. He's a graceful rotator who could grow into meaningful power if he gets stronger as he matures. He's an "Eye of the Beholder" over-slot candidate for the second or third round of the draft.

Comeau climbed Draft boards with a strong finish to the showcase circuit, batting a combined .417 with four extra-base hits in 10 games between the Area Code Games and the World Wood Bat Association World Championship. In between, he participated in the Canadian Futures Showcase and finished second in the Home Run Derby at Rogers Centre. He won't turn 18 until a month after the 2026 Draft, adding to his appeal. Comeau is very advanced at the plate for his age, employing a quick and effortless left-handed stroke while making good swing decisions. He's underdeveloped physically at 6-foot-4 and 190 pounds, so he's only scratching the surface of his power potential. He already shows precocious feel for driving balls to the opposite field and could provide 20-25 homers on an annual basis once he adds needed strength and pulls more pitches. Because he's a below-average runner, Comeau has limited defensive options. The Texas A&M recruit won't stick at shortstop, with third base his best-case scenario and the outfield corners not much of an option unless he gets quicker as he gets stronger. He has been clocked up to 92 mph on the mound, so arm strength isn't an issue.

The son of Hall of Famer Jim Thome, who's also an assistant coach for his Nazareth Academy (La Grange Park, Ill.) team, Landon is one of the best all-around hitters in the 2026 high school crop. Some scouts were more impressed with him last spring than his teammate Jaden Fauske, who signed with the White Sox for $2,997,500 as the top pick in the second round. Thome could go in the same range despite questions about his eventual defensive home. Thome turns his left-handed swing loose with maximum intent but has the pitch recognition and bat-to-ball skills to make a lot of hard contact. His stroke has loft geared to drive balls in the air and he has tapped into more power as he has improved his strength and bat speed. His pure hitting ability may stand out a little more than his pop, but both grade as at least solid. Thome is a below-average runner who could lose a step as he continues to fill out. He's a reliable defender with sure hands at shortstop, but his lack of quickness and fringy to average arm won't allow him to stay there at his next step, whether that be college at Florida State or pro ball. After working with Jake Cronenworth during the winter, he's moving and throwing better, giving him a better chance of playing second or third base. Scouts praise his baseball IQ and makeup.

Mendes came out of the very successful Jesuit High School program in Tampa and began his career at Mississippi. After a year pitching almost exclusively out of the bullpen, Mendes returned to his home state to join Florida State’s rotation. It was an up-and-down sophomore season, though he did pitch eight strong innings in a Regional win to help send the Seminoles to a Super Regional for the second straight year. He’s taken a very nice step forward as FSU’s Friday night starter in 2026, launching him into early-round consideration. An athletic 6-foot-1 left-hander, Mendes will use a robust five-pitch mix to keep hitters guessing. While his fastball sits around 92 mph and tops out at 96, it does feature some life upstairs with some angle to his glove side. His 80-mph changeup is his best secondary, a plus cambio he sells well with arm speed, the kind of offspeed offering that seems to pause in mid-air with late arm side depth to it. His low-80s slider can show some good short glove side tilt and he can back foot it to right-handed hitters and he’s added a new, harder cutter, with better shape and control of it as the season has gone on. He’ll use his upper-70s curve to steal a strike early in counts. Mendes has improved his delivery as well as his ability to control his emotions on the mound, all allowing him to minimize damage and fill up the strike zone a lot more consistently than in the past. He can run into trouble deeper in outings, but it’s not anything teams viewing him as a future big league starter to select in the top couple of rounds are overly concerned about.

The nephew of long-time big leaguer Sean Rodriguez, Williamson has been a member of the starting outfield at Central Florida pretty much since the start of his freshman year in 2024. That first season was fairly nondescript, but an MVP turn in the wood bat Cal Ripken League that summer led to a big step forward as a sophomore with the Knights. He finished the 2025 season with an 1.110 OPS, 13 homers and 13 steals, putting him in position to join former UCF teammate Antonio Jimenez, a third-rounder of the Mets last year, as an early-round selection. Williamson is a strong and compact left-handed hitter who gives off some Alek Thomas or Nate McLouth type vibes. He has the chance to hit, with some power, showing a solid overall approach that led to small strikeout and high walk rates in '25. There’s a little hitch in his swing at the start, with a drop in his hands and a barrel tilt that can affect his timing, leading some to worry a little bit about his hit tool. But he has a quick swing with plenty of bat speed, and he’s shown he can get to his solid raw pop in games, particularly to his pull side. An above-average runner who didn’t get thrown out in 13 attempts to steal a year ago, Williamson played center as a freshman but moved to right field last year and is likely to stay in a corner in 2026. He has the arm to profile well there, but a team interested in taking him could very well give him the chance to play up the middle, which would raise his profile.

As a junior, Clark hit .411 hitting leadoff and playing shortstop for St. John Bosco high school in California, earning MVP honors in the ultra-competitive Trinity League. He continued to perform over the summer at events like the Area Code Games and also helped Team USA take home a Gold Medal at the WSBC U-18 World Cup in Japan. He didn’t play a ton over the fall, but that did little to disrupt his upward momentum, and a strong start to his spring didn't hurt, either. But some struggles as his senior season wore on impacted his stock a bit. Clark has an exciting combination of upside and instincts. He’s a left-handed hitter who consistently makes excellent swing decisions. He doesn’t chase and routinely squares up the baseball with plus bat speed. While he’s pure hit and approach over power right now, there is some conviction that his ability to drive the ball will continue to show up as he moves along in the game. He’s a plus runner, and that tool plays up even more because of his high baseball IQ. The only thing scouts aren’t sure about regarding Clark is his ability to stick at shortstop long term. Teams interested in him early will certainly give him the chance to play the premium position, where his instincts and accurate arm play well, but some think second or third base might be a better fit long-term. He’s now committed to Duke for college, where he would get the chance to keep playing with his twin brother, Miles.

Scouts rated Radel as South Dakota's top high school prospect in 2024, though he didn't draw enough interest to divert him from Notre Dame. He immediately became a weekend starter for the Fighting Irish and has improved steadily throughout his three years in South Bend. He has added a couple of ticks of velocity and picked up a cutter as a junior, allowing him to miss more bats than ever and giving him a chance to become Notre Dame's first pitching first-rounder since Aaron Heilman in 2001. Radel's riding fastball now sits at 93-95 mph and touches 98 while holding velocity deep into games. He's doing a better job of locating a mid-80s slider with depth that has become a solid offering, while his new upper-80s cutter elicits plenty of chases. He lands his 78-82 mph curveball for strikes and mixes in an upper-80s changeup with fade and sink against left-handers. Though Radel doesn't have a true plus offering and his pitch shapes are fairly ordinary, he succeeds because of his pitchability and competitiveness. Combining a high release point with good extension gives batters a different look and he pounds the strike zone. He's a high-floor starter who could fit into the middle of a rotation.

Peterson is a hard-swinging third base prospect who has short levers for a 6-foot-3 hitter. There are times when his swing is out of control, but he still managed an 80% contact rate on the showcase circuit and he has enough power to threaten fences in all directions. A slick third base defender with a well-rounded, lefty-hitting skill set, Peterson has a shot to go toward the back of the first round.

The best Kansas prep position prospect since Bubba Starling went fifth overall to the Royals in 2011, Peterson won the High School Home Run Derby during All-Star Week and performed well at most showcase events last summer. He entered 2026 as one of the top power hitters in the high school class but isn't driving the ball with authority as much this spring. He would draw some interest as a pitching prospect if he didn't have so much offensive potential. Peterson is employing a selective approach, keeping his left-handed swing under control and utilizing the entire field. He still possesses plus raw power but is focusing on making line-drive contract. Once he learns to drive balls in the air more regularly, he could produce 20-25 homers per season. Peterson has slowed down as he has gotten stronger and is now a below-average runner. There are mixed opinions about his defense at third base, with some scouts believing he's fine there and others questioning his athleticism and envisioning him as more of a corner outfielder. His arm strength is beyond reproach because the Texas recruit has been clocked up to 94 mph on the mound, where he also has displayed an interesting low-80s slider.

After helping Liberty Christian Academy win a state title in Virginia as a junior in high school, Blair stayed put for college ball, immediately impacting the Liberty University pitching staff as a freshman reliever who earned Conference USA all-freshman team honors. He moved into the rotation as a sophomore in 2025 and was named to CUSA’s all-conference first team, and he’s upped his game even more in leading the Flames as their Friday night starter, vaulting him up Draft boards in the process. Blair offers an intriguing combination of funk, deception, stuff and command, with as many as five pitches to choose from. He’ll throw both a four-seam, with decent run to the glove side, and a two-seam with sink to the arm side, firing his fastball up to 97 mph. The sinker is a true bowling ball which was getting ground-ball outs around 50 percent of the time in 2026. He has a distinct slider, with bite, depth and occasional sweep, missing bats at around 83-84 mph, and more of an upper-80s cutter with short, late life. He doesn’t use his mid-80s changeup much, but some scouts think it could be solid average in time. All of Blair’s stuff plays up because of his unorthodox mechanics. His delivery features a low slot and cross-body arm action to go along with a leg kick. It looks like it should take a lot of effort, but he repeats it well and has become an extreme strike-thrower, creating a very uncomfortable at-bat. Not all teams will like the arm action, but his ability to take the ball every week this year with positive results should have him off the board in the top two rounds.

Not to be confused with the former Georgia safety with a similar name and build, Jackson spent his first college season at Wofford, winning Southern Conference freshman of the year honors and helping the Terriers earn their first-ever NCAA Tournament victory in 2024. After splitting time between the outfield, catcher and DH for the Bulldogs as a sophomore, he became a full-time backstop and has exploded this spring. The first catcher in Division I history to total 25 homers and 25 steals in the same season, he earned the Southeastern Conference player of the year and tournament MVP awards and led the league in all three triple crown categories entering NCAA tournament play. Jackson is extremely strong and hits the ball extremely hard from the right side of the plate, looking like a taller version of Tyler O'Neill. He has demonstrated a selective approach throughout his college career and is doing a much better job this year of making contact, both against velocity and against non-fastballs. There's still some swing-and-miss to his game but he's getting to his well-above-average power more consistently and crushing homers from foul pole to foul pole. More athletic than most catchers, Jackson can flash plus speed and regularly posts average run times. He's still a work in progress behind the plate with the potential to become a fringy or perhaps average defender once he polishes his receiving and blocking. He features solid raw arm strength but throws with effort and needs to improve his technique and accuracy. If he can't stay behind the plate, he could handle the outfield corners in pro ball.

Back in the late 1990s, Howard Horn was a part of the same Princeton pitching staff that featured future big leaguer and current Rangers general manager Chris Young. Howard's son, Archer, has become one of the more intriguing prospects in Northern California, a two-way player who most think has a brighter future as a position player after displaying his skillset over the summer at events like Perfect Game National and the Area Code Games. Horn joins Tyler Spangler as left-handed-hitting NorCal prep shortstops getting a lot of attention. While Spangler is the more highly regarded prospect, Horn might be a bit more explosive, albeit less polished. At the plate, he shows off good bat speed and the ability to loft the baseball, providing some confidence that he’ll impact the ball with high exit velocities, especially as he adds strength. Though not everyone loves his pure hit tool, there could very well be more power to come in the future. Horn is an average runner but is a good athlete who has been his school’s point guard on the basketball court in the past. He’s 93-95 mph off the mound, and that arm really works from shortstop. Some see a move to third or second in the future given his lack of pure footspeed, but refinement and consistency on his angles and transfers could give him a chance to stick. Both he and Spangler are committed to Stanford for college ball.

Horn is an average runner but is a good athlete who has been his school’s point guard on the basketball court in the past. He’s 93-95 mph off the mound, and that arm really works from shortstop. Some see a move to third or second in the future given his lack of pure footspeed, but refinement and consistency on his angles and transfers could give him a chance to stick. Both he and Spangler are committed to Stanford for college ball.

Doug Waechter grew up in the Tampa-St. Pete area then went on to pitch for parts of six seasons in the big leagues, five of them with the hometown Rays after they took him in the third round of the 1999 Draft. His son, Kaden, has a chance to go earlier than that, a product of the same Jesuit High School in Tampa that produced future big league right-handers like Brad Radke and Lance McCullers Jr. Waechter offers an exciting combination of MLB family ties, projection in a 6-foot-3 frame, athleticism and feel for pitching. His fastball typically registers average velocities, sitting around 93 mph, though he can reach back for 95-96 mph, and there could be more in the tank to come. It plays up because it has good life to it, and he can command it to both sides of the plate. His top secondary offering right now is a slider that works best as an out pitch in the 84-86 mph range. He’ll crank it up a bit and turn the pitch into an upper-80s cutter, and he has some feel for a changeup, though he can drop his elbow on it at times. All of Waechter’s arsenal comes from an easy and repeatable delivery. He’s willing to throw all of his offerings at any point, pitching backwards when he needs to, filling up the zone consistently. Ceiling and pitchability don’t often come in one package, and that’s why scouts will be watching this Florida State recruit very carefully in the spring.

Grahovac is a physical 3B/OF who hit 23 homers as a freshman despite whiffing a ton. As a sophomore, he played just six games before tearing the labrum in his left shoulder, which required surgery. He's a high-variance 2026 prospect who had strikeout risk prior to the injury.

The cousin of Brewers outfielder Garrett Mitchell, Grahovac was a mainstay on the showcase circuit last summer and a member of USA Baseball’s gold medal-winning 18U team. A standout at Villa Park High School in California, a school that has produced big league talent like Aaron Boone and Mark Trumbo, Grahovac has continued to show some offensive potential this spring, albeit with continuing concerns about his future profile. Grahovac shows off a lot of strength from the right side of the plate, with plenty of present power that showed up at times over the summer and this spring. But it’s strength over bat speed, and there’s continued to be too much swing-and-miss, with scouts worrying about his hit tool. His approach and bat path are not conducive to high contact rates. There is also uncertainty over where Grahovac will play defensively. He’s a decent athlete who plays shortstop in high school, but the Texas A&M recruit won’t play there at the next level. Most see a move to third or left field as the best option, and he’s told teams he’s willing to catch. While he hasn’t seen much time back there, it could be the spot where he profiles best.

Hirschkorn's coordination for an athlete his size is remarkable, and the 6-foot-7 righty is able to locate his plus-flashing slider with mature precision and consistency. These gyro sliders enjoy a little extra depth thanks to his remarkable size, as well as his feel for spotting it. The rest of Hirschkorn's repertoire is below average, and his fastball was only sitting 93 with downhill angle last summer. There may eventually be an offspeed pitch here because Hirschkorn's feel for pitching is very special for a high schooler his size. Right now, he looks more like a Jonathan Bowlan starter kit than a righty CC Sabathia or anything like that.

The Northern California high school scene hasn't produced a first-round arm since Matt Manning went No. 9 overall to the Tigers back in 2016. That dry stretch could end in 2026 with Hirschkorn. He didn't enter the summer that high on radars, but he certainly ended it firmly on the map, especially with outstanding performances at Perfect Game National and the Area Code Games, showing off a combination of size, athleticism and projection. Standing at 6-foot-7, Hirschkorn is an athletic right-hander with the chance to have a legitimate three-pitch mix. It's easy gas, up to 95-96 mph with very little effort, and it plays well at the top of the zone. There's a ton of room to get bigger and stronger, making it easy to dream of triple digits in the future. He backs it up with a very good low-80s slider that misses a ton of bats. There is some feel for a mid-80s changeup, but he hasn't thrown it a ton yet. Over the winter, scouts might check in to watch Hirschkorn's athleticism on the court during basketball season. That part of his game is apparent in his ability to repeat his delivery and fill up the zone, though some might quibble with a little high elbow. He's not done a lot of work in terms of pitch design, adding even more upside potential for the LSU recruit. He's reminded some of Noble Meyer, a 2023 high schooler from the Pacific Northwest who ended up going No. 10 overall in that Draft.

Only one player in Central Florida was named both an All-American and a Gold Glove winner by the American Baseball Coaches Association. That was Head, the top player in the Orlando area who helped lead his Windermere High School team to a regional championship its first appearance in the state Class 7A finals for the first time in school history. The Orange County male athlete of the year also caught the attention of scouts, who like his combination of tools and makeup. The first thing that might stand out with Head is his athletic 6-foot-3 frame. He’s a left-handed hitter and thrower with instincts on both sides of the ball. Right now, he’s more hit over power with a solid approach and a feel for making consistent contact. There is some question about how much power he’ll have, as he didn’t always show enough impact, but it’s not hard to dream on more pop to come as he physically matures. He’s an aggressive and savvy baserunner who can steal some bags. Right now, Head is athletic enough to play center field and was recognized for his glove work this spring. While his instincts should allow him to stay up the middle initially, there are some who feel he might continue to slow down and will have to shift to an outfield corner. That would put more pressure on that projectable power to show up on the regular. Teams considering him on Day 2 of the Draft will be buying the North Carolina State recruit’s upside, work ethic and overall baseball IQ.

Brown comes from a Sulphur (La.) HS program that has sent four pitchers to the big leagues, headlined by John Thomson. A key starter for the U.S. national team that won the 18-and-under World Cup last September, he's one of the most polished high school arms in the Draft. But his stuff hasn't taken a step forward this spring, so it may be difficult for clubs to select Gatorade's state player of the year high enough to divert him from his Louisiana State commitment. Brown's fastball typically ranges from 88-92 mph and peaks at 94, but it plays better than its velocity thanks to low release height and carry as well as his ability to command the heater. He can land his sweeping 78-82 mph slider for strikes or get hitters to chase it off the plate. He can fade or sink a changeup with similar velocity, and he has the faith to throw it in any count. Brown is also a quality athlete who doubles as a center fielder and one of the best prep hitters in Louisiana. He hides the ball well in his low-effort delivery and moves his pitches around the strike zone with ease. He might make a push for the first round with more velocity and there's definitely more projection remaining in his 6-foot-2 frame.

The son of former big leaguer Jose Contreras, Joseph's velocity has been growing for the last couple of years and was parked in the 94-97 mph range at the start of the 2026 season. He has his father’s forkball, which has devastating sink. Teams are focused on deciphering whether or not they think Contreras’ delivery is sustainable for a starter, and if not, how they might augment it. Right now, it's a stiff, upright delivery with a very high slot. It doesn't look like a starter's motion, but Contreras has good feel for locating his 82-84 mph slider on the edge of the zone. Contreras might end up with an elite secondary pitch in that forkball, and he has enough feel for location to develop as a starter even though his delivery doesn't look like it will allow him to throw strikes.

The son of former All-Star José Contreras, Joseph inherited his father's 6-foot-4 frame and aptitude for throwing a forkball. He helped Blessed Trinity HS (Roswell, Ga.) win the state 4-A title in 2025 while his velocity and prospect stock were making significant jumps. He could fit into the top two rounds as one of the higher-ceiling arms in the high school class, though teams will have to sign him away from a Vanderbilt commitment. After topping out at 91 mph in 2024, Contreras now works at 92-95 and peaks at 98 with his four-seam fastball, though it doesn't stand out in terms of life or shape. He did manage to jam Aaron Judge with a 94-mph heater and induce a broken-bat double play while pitching for Brazil during the World Baseball Classic. He still has room to pack plenty of muscle on his lanky frame, so he could add more power to his heater and his secondary offerings. His best pitch is a 77-81 mph forkball that dies at the plate, though both his 82-85 mph slider and 80-83 mph changeup with fade are solid weapons as well. Contreras has a clean arm action and delivers his pitches from a high three-quarters slot with short extension, creating some reliever risk. He throws his fastball for strikes and gets chases with the rest of his arsenal, though he still requires more polish. He needs to improve the quality and command with his heater and show that his forkball, slider and changeup will work against more discerning hitters.

After helping his high school win an Oregon state title in 2023, Kleinschmit went the junior college route, spending a year and earning All-American status at Linn-Benton Community College. He made a seamless transition into Oregon State’s rotation in 2025, striking out 11.2 K/9 and holding hitters to a .194 batting average. More success pitching on the weekends for the Beavers could help him be one of the first college lefties to come off the board in July. During his first season in Corvallis, Kleinschmit showed the ability to fill up the strike zone with three pitches. While he won’t overwhelm anyone with pure stuff, he makes up for it with movement and feel for pitching. His fastball typically sat in the 90-93 mph range in 2025, topping out at 95 mph, with good tailing life and scouts wonder what an uptick in velocity might do for his profile, a la Red Sox lefty Connelly Early. He has good rotation and depth with his upper-70s slurvy slider to go along with decent feel and deception with his low-80s changeup. Early’s step forward stuff wise came with added strength and there’s the potential for Kleinschmit to go in that direction especially once he gets into pro ball. He has a solid starting pitcher’s foundation with his pitch mix and ability to be around the zone and if he manages to find more in the tank this spring, he’ll be on a more upward trajectory on Draft boards.

Hughes led Stetson in slugging (.515) as a freshman in 2024 before transferring to Texas Tech, where he batted .327/.411/.697 with nearly as many homers (19) as strikeouts (24) last spring. He continued to control the strike zone and hit the ball hard in the Cape Cod League, where he earned All-Star accolades and helped Bourne win its third title in four years. He's an offensive-minded left fielder who draws comparisons to Rusty Greer and Athletics 2025 second-round pick Devin Taylor. Hughes scores well analytically because he makes good swing decisions and a lot of contact against all types of pitches, producing a lot of hard line drives. He has a pretty left-handed swing that's compact and quick, and he possesses plus raw power. With his hitting ability, he should be able to make adjustments to allow him to launch balls to his pull side more frequently and get to 20-25 homers per season. He'll have to produce at the plate because Hughes doesn't offer much value elsewhere. He's a below-average runner with arm strength to match, which limits his defensive options. He can look shaky at times in left field, and at 5-foot-11, he lacks the ideal size for first base.

A .334/.407/.483 hitter in two years at Cal (and a .380/.442/.439 hitter across two seasons on Cape Cod), Advincula transferred to Georgia Tech for his draft year. He's got one of the better pure hit tools in the 2026 draft, tracking pitches like a hawk and moving his barrel all over the zone to spoil tough pitches and slice singles and doubles into play. He's a chase-prone hitter who offers at too many secondary pitches below the zone, but Advincula finds a way to put the barrel on them anyway. Though he has a slasher's approach to hitting, Advincula isn't a little guy, he's an even six feet tall with below-average raw power. It's no big juice, but it's enough not to drag down the way his hit tool plays. Advincula has only played second base in college, but is athletic and rangy and might be able to run around in the outfield, if not play a second infield position. He has a shot to be an Adam Frazier type of everyday second baseman.

Advincula established himself as one of college baseball's best contact hitters in two seasons at California, batting .334 with a 9 percent strikeout rate. He made an even bigger name for himself in the Cape Cod League, winning the batting title (.392) in 2024 and the top pro prospect award voted on by scouts last summer. Afterward, he transferred to Georgia Tech, where he ranks first in Division I in hits (103) and third in batting (.431) at the outset of NCAA tournament play and further helped his cause by hitting .477 in Atlantic Coast Conference games. Advincula is a master of reading defenses and using his short left-handed swing to slap balls through holes for hits. His bat-to-ball skills can work against him at times because he does chase pitches out of the zone, leading to suboptimal contact and cutting into his walk totals. He shows enough bat speed and strength to provide double-digit home run power, but he has gone deep just once in 205 at-bats in the wood-bat Cape League because he rarely turns on pitches or lifts them in the air. Though he can produce well-above-average home-to-first times as he dashes out of the batter's box, Advincula plays more as a plus runner and isn't a prolific basestealer. He has good infield actions and quickness but just fringy arm strength, making him best suited for second base, where he's a sure-handed defender. The Yellow Jackets tried him at shortstop in the fall, but his arm was stretched on the left side of the infield.

Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Cutter: 50 | Splitter: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 50 Known more as a slugging third baseman for much of his high school career, Brown has dramatically improved on the mound this spring. He has added significant strength as a senior, pushing his fastball to 98 mph as the highlight of a power four-pitch arsenal. He'll get the chance to play both ways if he attends Mississippi State but is more likely to focus on pitching after turning pro for a seven-figure bonus. Brown can work in the mid-90s with some armside run on his heater and maintain his velocity deep into starts, though his fastball gets hit more than it should and he'll need to tweak its shape to maximize its effectiveness. He has the makings of a plus low-80s slider with sweeping action and also utilizes an upper-80s cutter. He does a nice job of killing spin on a mid-80s splitter that he employs as a changeup. Brown has a strong 6-foot-4 frame and operates with little effort from a low arm slot and wide angle. He has the ingredients for average or better control once he gains more experience. Some evaluators worry that his long arm action and tendency to open up in his delivery pose reliever risk, while others believe he can clean that up as he focuses on pitching. He's just scratching the surface of his potential and could develop into a mid-rotation starter.

A majority of big league talent to be drafted out of British Columbia in Canada has been of the position player variety, with Tyler O’Neill and Brett Lawrie the most recent top three round success stories. The last time a high school pitcher went early from the province was back in 2002 when left-hander Adam Loewen was the No. 4 overall pick in the Draft. A fellow southpaw, Duncan looked like he had a very good chance to end that drought, first exciting scouts after throwing well at various showcase events last summer and fall, then standing out this spring during trips to Arizona in Florida. He walked off the mound with an elbow injury during a spring outing with Team Canada in the Dominican Republic, and though it was confirmed in early June that he would require Tommy John surgery, the industry was still bullish on him being drafted and signed. A projectable 6-foot-3 lefty, Duncan has shown steady progress stuff-wise while being in front of scouts a lot since age 14 pitching for Canada’s junior national team. He was sitting around 88-89 mph with his fastball then and kind hovered in that range, with scouts waiting for a leap forward. It’s possible that started to happen at the Futures Showcase, when he was up to 95 mph -- sitting 93 -- with his heater. He’s also shown the ability to show off at least above-average secondary stuff, really selling his deceptive changeup with excellent arm speed and snapping off very good breaking stuff when he stays on top of it. Not only does Duncan have a true three-pitch mix (it's not too difficult to dream about three above-average-to-plus offerings in the future), he’s shown a propensity for strike-throwing and understanding how to mix all of his pitches. He’s committed to Vanderbilt for college, but there was conviction he would still go in the first few rounds and rehab his elbow under pro instruction.

South Carolina features two high school position players who could factor in the top 50 selections, though scouts are split as to which is better. Some prefer Bo Lowrance's hitting ability, while other lean toward Marchand's superior all-around tools and defensive value. The latter helped James Island HS (Charleston) win the state 4-A title as a sophomore and the 5-A Division I championship as a junior, and he should become his school's first Draft pick since 1969 Seattle Pilots first-rounder Gorman Thomas. Thanks to Marchand's quick right-handed stroke and still-growing strength, balls jump off his bat when he times them right. He tends to lunge forward at the plate and hit off his front foot, though he manages to keeps his hands back and has a strong record of production on the showcase circuit. He could develop 25-homer power if he smooths out his swing and turns on more pitches. Marchand's hands work well in the field as well as at the plate, allowing him to get rid of balls quickly at shortstop. Clocked up to 92 mph on the mound, the Mississippi recruit has plus arm strength, good defensive instincts and a chance to remain at short. He has merely average speed and quickness, so he could end up at second or third base.

Lord is a XXL righty with a good (albeit slightly slow) slider that features plus depth in the 77-79 mph range. For how big Lord is, he is very coordinated and balanced throughout his delivery and is likely to throw starter-quality strikes with his fastball and slider. His changeup flashes bat-missing sink, but only once every 10 or so attempts. His size creates downhill plane on his fastball that might make it vulnerable to damage if Lord only ever sits 93, but he's a good athlete for his size and should grow into better velocity as he matures. He looks like an innings-eating no. 4/5 starter.

The Florida panhandle is often a difficult area to get scouted due to its remote location. But evaluators will be spending plenty of time there just to see the pitching staff at South Walton High School. It’s a group led by Coleman Borthwick, transfer Griffin Loy and Lord, a super-projectable right-hander whose size and stuff certainly garnered attention during the summer showcase circuit at events like the East Coast Professional Showcase and MLB’s High School All-American Game. Lord is a tall and lanky 6-foot-8 right-hander with serious projection. His fastball will sit around 94 mph, though he’s shown the ability to reach back for 97-98 mph in shorter stints, and he throws it with heavy sink. At times, he can really snap off a plus upper-70s curveball, though he can try to do too much with it and it becomes slurvy. He doesn’t need a changeup in high school, but he did show a low-80s one occasionally over the summer, though it’s more of a batting practice fastball than anything truly effective. All of Lord’s arsenal comes from a fast, easy arm and it’s easy to dream on more velocity to come as he fills out that frame and learns to sync up his delivery consistently, which should also help his command. He did have Tommy John surgery as a freshman but has shown no ill effects now. He switched his college commitment from Florida to Mississippi State and will play for Brian O’Connor should the Draft not go his way.

Bowen is a muscular, physically mature corner outfield prospect who is already generating plus bat speed. His swing is a little too awkward looking to accept that his showcase contact performance (76%, average) will hold in pro ball.

There is a constant desire for baseball to attract more athletes to the game, and the scouting industry has the chance to do just that with Bowen. The JSerra Catholic standout entered the summer as a former football player with raw tools and finished it rushing up Draft boards because of more confidence in his ability to use those tools with outstanding performances at showcase events like the Area Code Games. Bowen is a veritable toolshed in a strong, athletic 6-foot-3 package. A football standout who is now focusing on baseball only, he’s a physical right-handed hitter who has always been able to punish the baseball. It might be 70-grade raw power, but the question in the past was if he would hit enough to get to it. There’s been in-zone swing-and-miss in the past, but he found the barrel a lot more consistently over the summer, leading evaluators to be more bullish on his hitability. With plus athleticism that plays on the basepaths and in the outfield, Bowen has the chance to stick in center field, though he has the plus arm to profile well in right field if needed. He also gets high marks for his makeup and high energy play on the field. If the hit tool keeps improving, the Oregon State recruit could easily skyrocket into the first round.

There has never been a high schooler from Vermont to get drafted and make it to the big leagues in the six decades since the Draft was instituted. Only two have ever been selected in the top five rounds, most recently when the Pirates took Owen Kellington in the fourth round of the 2021 Draft. McCarthy moved up his own timetable to join this select group when he reclassified in January to join the Class of 2026. While McCarthy is a bit undersized at 6-foot even, he's strong and extremely athletic on the mound and has shown at least glimpses of four potentially plus future pitches. He'll throw both a four-seam fastball up in the zone and a two-seamer with hard sink, popping some at 99 mph, sitting around 96 mph. His changeup might be his best secondary offering at present, sold with very deceptive arm speed and featuring solid late fade. He'll show off two distinct breaking pitches, with a sweeper of a slider at around 88 mph and a power downer low-80s curveball. With a super fast arm and his athleticism on the mound, McCarthy repeats his delivery well and throws a decent amount of strikes. The one thing he lacks is track record; he wasn't on the 2025 summer showcase circuit with his new class because he didn't reclassify until the winter. He opened a ton of eyes with an early start in Florida, then tried to do too much in his first start up north, with evaluators trying to figure out a bit of an irregular pitching schedule for the Tennessee recruit as the weather warmed up.

Volchko was an electric, hard-throwing high school righty from Northern California who struggled in two seasons at Stanford (he had an ERA over 6.00 as a soph) and transferred to Georgia. At his best, Volchko has a hairy mid-90s fastball, plus cutter/slider, and a firm, low-90s changeup with sink and tail. His fastball's movement does not allow that pitch to miss bats. The possibility that a change of scenery will help his stuff play better is why Volchko is speculatively ranked here.

The best player to come out of Redwood High School in Visalia, California, has been infielder Aaron Hill, though he went on to spend three years at Louisiana State before starting his pro career. Hill was drafted out of high school in the sixth round and it looks like based on talent, Volchko could go much earlier than that after popping up in a big way this spring. Volchko is big and projectable at 6-foot-4, reminding some of a young Noah Syndergaard with a high-waisted frame, and he has the chance to have a legitimate four-pitch mix. Coming from a high overhead slot, he’s thrown his fastball in the 92-96 mph range. His upper-80s slider should be a plus pitch that misses bats, but his 82-85 mph curve is also an effective breaker. His firm 87-88 mph changeup is behind, but he has feel for that pitch as well. While he’s a good athlete who tunnels his pitches well, scouts wonder about Volchko’s ability to throw anything with arm-side run from that slot. His strike-throwing has been inconsistent at times, though improvements in that area this spring are a big reason for his helium. Scouts were streaming in to see whether it might be worth trying to sign him away from his commitment to Stanford.

Johnson has incredible hand speed and managed an 84% contact rate during two years on the showcase circuit even though his swing often has bad footwork and balance. There are times when Johnson totally cuts his stride, robs himself of athleticism, and yet still stings the baseball because of how much power he's able to generate with his hands and wrists. Pro instruction might coax out a better, more stable offensive player. Even though Johnson's hands on the infield are bad enough that he's projected to the outfield here, his potential hit/power combo gives him the ceiling of a heart-of-the-order hitter.

Johnson has been a famous prospect for years and won Gatorade's Georgia high school player of the year award as a junior last spring, but he presents a conundrum for scouts. They like the player more than his tools and his profile, and he regressed on the showcase circuit last summer after standing out there in 2024. It's unclear whether he'll get drafted high enough to divert him from a Vanderbilt commitment. Johnson takes better at-bats and makes contact more easily than most high school players. His right-handed swing can get too rotational at times, and he didn't do much damage against quality pitching during the summer, still putting the ball in play but producing too many rolled-over grounders. He does feature plenty of bat speed and strength, and his biggest proponents hope he can make adjustments and turn into a solid hitter with average power. As he has matured physically, Johnson has slowed down and now has below-average speed at best. He nevertheless has a chance to remain at shortstop, where his fluid actions and advanced instincts translate into surprising range. He has quick hands and solid arm strength, which would allow him to make an easy transition to third base if needed.

Kennedy may be the most improved player in NCAA Division I this season. After batting .209 as a freshman at Texas in 2024 and topping the Big 12 Conference with 79 strikeouts in 2025 at Kansas State, he had LASIK surgery. Better vision has led to increased frequency and quality of contact, allowing him to earn Cape Cod League all-star honors last summer and eclipse the Wildcats' single-season home run record 20 this spring. Now that he's seeing the ball so much better, Kennedy is chasing fewer pitches and controlling the strike zone. While the right-handed hitter still will fish for some curveballs out of the zone, he has gone from being helpless against curves and sliders to crushing them. He's pulling balls in the air much more frequently than in the past, hitting them harder and generating plus raw power seemingly with just a flick of his wrist. Kennedy offers plenty of athleticism to go with his improved offensive profile. He shows solid speed out of the batter's box and even more quickness once he accelerates. A second baseman as a freshman and third baseman as a sophomore, he has upgraded his actions and lateral range at shortstop, where he displays solid arm strength.

Bailey worked just 23 2/3 innings at McLennan (Texas) CC before tearing the anterior cruciate ligament and meniscus in his left knee on March 4, ending his sophomore season. But that was more than enough to affirm his status as the top junior college prospect in the 2026 Draft, and he still could go as high as the second round following knee surgery. After spending 2025 at Baylor, he initially committed to Texas A&M before joining the Highlanders. Bailey works with a 93-96 mph fastball that touches 98 with sink that elicits more grounders than swings and misses. His 82-85 mph breaking ball can fluctuate between a curveball and slider and is most effective when it has tighter break. Both are solid offerings with the potential to get better, as is his mid-80s changeup with fade and tumble. A quality athlete who gets down the mound well, Bailey has some effort in his delivery but improved his strike throwing before he got hurt. There's projection remaining in his 6-foot-3 frame, so he could add some more power to his pitches. If he turns pro, he should be ready to return to the mound around the start of next season. He missed his junior year in high school while recovering from Tommy John surgery.

Riojas won 15 games in two years as a reliever at Texas-San Antonio before transferring to Texas, where he worked his way into the rotation by mid-2025. He was pitching himself toward the top three rounds before coming down with the flu and bronchitis, costing him 20 pounds and sapping his stuff as he surrendered 27 runs in 14 2/3 innings over his final starts. After going unselected last July, he has emerged as one of the best senior prospects in the 2026 Draft. By regaining the weight he lost and adding another 10 pounds, Riojas boosted his four-seam fastball 2-3 mph to parking at 94-96 and peaking at 98 with carry. His heater has been unhittable while he has commanded it to both sides of the plate this spring. He uses a diving 82-85 mph splitter as his changeup and it has been just as untouchable. His upper-80s cutter can be a plus pitch at its best, and he also deploys a sweepier mid-80s slider and a low-80s curveball. Riojas will unleash four-seamers, curveballs, cutters and splitters from a high three-quarters arm slot, then mix in two-seamers and sliders from a lower angle. He pounds the zone with his entire arsenal, and all of his pitches save his slider elicit plenty of chases as well. The only real knocks on him are that he's not terribly deceptive and he'll turn 23 on Draft Day, but he's advanced enough to make his pro debut in Double-A and could help a big league rotation in a hurry.

Sims looks like an NBA wing player on the mound at an ultra-long 6-foot-8. He doesn't yet have total control of his body and scatters his upper-90s fastball all over the place. Even though Sims' body isn't often well-connected throughout his delivery, he's still touching 100 pretty regularly and will likely throw even harder as he continues to fill out, especially if he eventually shifts into relief. Sims' slider has big depth and finish in the dirt to his glove side; it's a future plus pitch and will probably be his best one at peak. It will be a challenge for a pro dev group to take the raw material here (freaky size, arm speed, and a great slider) and see if it can be polished ito a late-inning diamond.

Sims has the most electric arm in the high school class and repeatedly pushed his fastball to 100 mph on the showcase circuit last summer. He also has a 6-foot-8, 205-pound frame with plenty of room to add strength, so there may be more velocity to come. After winning an Oklahoma state 6-A championship at Edmond Santa Fe HS last spring, he transferred to Prestonwood Christian Academy (Plano, Texas) to play his senior season for James Vilade, a former scout and pro and college coach. Sims previously worked from a three-quarters arm angle and topped out at 97 mph with more sink on his four-seamer. After raising his slot in the past year, he now operates at 94-97 and reaches triple digits with more carry. He generates outstanding velocity with arm speed and little effort, another reason to project future velocity gains. The rest of his arsenal needs work, because he lacks consistency with his shapes and control with his mid-80s slider and changeup. Sims still is learning to keep his extra-long limbs in sync in his delivery, and while he throws his heater for strikes, his fastball command is a work in progress. He'll require time to develop and comes with reliever risk but also immense arm talent. He'll turn 19 a month before the 2026 Draft and would be sophomore-eligible in 2028 if he follows through on his Oklahoma commitment.

When several heavy hitters came to Texas in February to scout college tournaments and some high school games, Harris dazzled them by striking out 17 in six no-hit innings. That outing was the first step in surpassing several more famous names to emerge as the consensus top mound prospect among Lone Star State prepsters. While he doesn't have the loudest stuff, he has feel for four pitches and has dominated all spring. Harris operates at 90-94 mph and reaches 96 with his fastball, displaying the ability to create carry, sink or cut while commanding it well. It could develop into a plus offering once it adds more power, as could his low-80s slider with high spin rates and flashes of two-plane depth. He lands a mid-70s curveball for strikes and has begun work on a mid-80s changeup. Harris has a projectable 6-foot-3 frame and, as one of the youngest pitchers in the Draft, plenty of time to add strength. The Texas recruit is athletic and moves well down the mound, creating good extension while easily repeating his delivery and pounding the strike zone. Assuming he turns pro as a top-two-rounds talent, he should advance quickly for a high schooler.

Holloway has revamped his mechanics after transferring from Nolensville (Tenn.) HS to Nashville's Christ Presbyterian Academy, where his pitching coach is former Cy Young Award winner R.A. Dickey. He's generating one of the best fastballs and some of the most effortless velocity in this Draft, though his lack of feel for a breaking ball is a concern. His stuff backed up briefly when he was hit in the head by an errant throw during practice in early April, but he was back to touching the upper 90s by the end of the month. After working with a 92-96 mph fastball that lacked life last summer, Holloway now owns a 94-98 mph heater that has peaked at 100 with improved command and tumbling action. He's still not displaying much aptitude for spin, flashing some decent mid-80s sliders but most often working with a below-average breaker. He has much more trust in a slightly harder changeup with depth. The 6-foot-5 Holloway has tightened up his delivery and is doing a better job of keeping his long limbs in sync and providing consistent strikes. Lowering his arm slot has helped the Vanderbilt commit improve the shape of his fastball and his ability to harness it. He's one of the more intriguing left-handers available, though he comes with significant reliever risk and plenty of divergent opinions on where he belongs in the Draft.

A high-leverage reliever at North Carolina State and with Team USA during his first two years in college, Dudan moved to the rotation this spring. The good news is that his fastball/slider combination remained dynamic in longer outings and he dramatically improved his control, making him a possible first-rounder. The bad news is that he blew out his elbow after throwing 116 pitches against Notre Dame on April 4 -- he hit 98 mph in the eighth inning -- and required Tommy John surgery. Dudan averaged 96 mph and touched 99 with his fastball as a junior, showing carry at times and sink at others, though his heater stands out more for its ability to generate groundouts than empty swings. His tight upper-80s slider is a legitimate wipeout pitch, producing a 41 percent chase rate and 48 percent swing-and-miss rate this spring. He also showed some feel for an upper-80s changeup with sink and fade, though he barely used it. A quality athlete, Dudan cut his walk rate from 15 percent in his first two seasons to 6 percent in 2026. While his aptitude for a changeup and improved control enhance his chances of succeeding as a starter, scouts believe his delivery with a long arm action and low slot makes him more likely to wind up as a reliever. He'll likely go in the second round even though he won't return to the mound until late 2027.

Tinney is a monstrous 6-foot-4 catcher who had a power-hitting breakout as a sophomore at Notre Dame, where he slugged .753 before entering the transfer portal and heading to Austin. Tinney has plus pull power and, especially after conference play began in 2025, he was among the college baseball leaders in hard-hit rate. He struggled to stay with sliders on Cape Cod and struck out nearly as much as he did during the regular season in half as many games. Tinney has big hit tool risk and needs refinement on defense, especially his framing.

Tinney earned All-America honors as a Notre Dame sophomore last spring, slashing .348/.498/.753 with 17 homers to stamp himself as one of the top catching prospects for 2026. His stock took a hit when batted .165 with a 40 percent strikeout rate in the wood-bat Cape Cod League and struggled during fall practice after transferring to Texas, but he has rebounded with a strong junior season. Few players in this Draft can match his combination of raw power and arm strength. At 6-foot-4 and 240 pounds and with a right-handed stroke geared to crush balls in the air to his pull side, Tinney is designed to hit home runs. He generates high-end exit velocities, but there are concerns about his hitting ability and how much of his double-plus raw pop he'll be able to get to in pro ball. He takes a lot of offspeed pitches for strikes and swings through a lot of offerings of all types in the zone, though he mitigates his excessive strikeouts with a healthy amount of walks. Tinney can flash well-above-average arm strength, though it plays more as plus and he needs to improve his transfer and the accuracy of his throws. He lacks quickness and agility behind the plate, though he has become a better receiver and framer this spring and perhaps can become average in both regards. His best-case scenario is that he becomes a larger version of Hunter Goodman.

Rutgers' regular catcher as a freshman in 2024, Natili has improved offensively and defensively in each of the last two years after transferring to Cincinnati. He ranked second in the Cape Cod League with six homers last summer and has continued to display some of the best power among the 2026 college catching crop this spring. He could become the Bearcats' highest pick since Ian Happ went ninth overall in 2015. Natili makes the most of his plus raw pop by launching balls in the air, and he has the ability to drive pitches out of the park to all fields. His right-handed swing can get too long, leading to swings and misses at an alarming number of fastballs, including in-zone heaters. He does mitigate that flaw with a relatively selective approach but always will be a power-over-hit guy. A well-below-average runner, Natili moves better behind the plate than he does on the bases. He's getting better as a receiver and blocker, leading to hope that he can become an average defender. His strong arm and leadership skills are assets.

Broussard is a plus-plus runner and plus contact hitter who tracks pitches well and hits with a style that takes advantage of his speed. He's a good center field defender and should at least be a good fourth outfielder, but he's also one of the younger college hitters in the entire 2026 draft class and might yet grow into a sneaky amount of power.

The toolsy Broussard has flown under the radar more than he should, going undrafted out of a suburban Houston high school in 2023 and again after batting .409 with 17 steals in 36 games at San Jacinto (Texas) JC a year later. He's still overshadowed a bit in a deep crop of Texas college outfielders but is beginning to shed his anonymity. He stood out with his athleticism last spring after transferring to Houston and won co-MVP honors in the Cape Cod League All-Star game last summer. Broussard's best tool is his plus-plus speed, and he looks to get the most out of it by making consistent contact from the left side of the plate. He has a reasonably disciplined approach and hits hard line drives from gap to gap. He features bat speed and wiry strength, and he generates some surprising exit velocities along with occasional opposite-field power for a player listed at 6 feet and 170 pounds. He added muscle before his junior season and won't turn 21 until two months after the Draft, so he has more projection remaining than most college players. An accomplished basestealer, Broussard swiped 41 bags in 45 attempts (91 percent) between Houston and the Cape in 2025. His speed also plays well in center field, where he's a quality defender. With average to solid arm strength, he's capable of fitting anywhere in the outfield.

Peterson recorded an immaculate inning during his first college start in 2024 and has been Sam Houston's Friday-night starter the last two seasons. Big league clubs had interest in signing him as a sophomore-eligible last year, but he turned down their overtures and went undrafted. His feel for spin and delivery metrics could allow him to join 1984 second-rounder Kevin Renz as the highest-drafted pitchers in Bearkats history. Peterson owns one of college baseball's best curveballs, a high-spin 79-82 mph hammer, and ratchets up the rpms on a solid low-80s slider as well. He also imparts high spin rates on a 91-94 mph fastball that tops out at 96, and it plays up a bit thanks to shape, command and deception. He barely uses a mid-80s changeup that needs a lot of work. If Peterson threw harder, he might be a first-rounder. He's an athletic mover who gets down the mound well, creating plenty of extension from a low release height. He not only throws strikes with all three of his primary offerings, but he also locates them well, enhancing his mid-rotation profile.

In 2022, Xavier Isaac was a big 6-foot-4 left-handed-hitting first baseman coming out of the Florida high school ranks, one who ended up being a surprise first-round selection of the Rays. Isaac has since reconfigured his body and proven the Rays right by being one of the better power-hitting prospects in the Minors. Could his path help Bailey, another 6-foot-4, lefty-swinging corner infielder also from the Florida prep scene? In some ways, Bailey is ahead of where Isaac was in his senior season. While Bailey is very physical, he’s more athletic than you might think when looking at him, while Isaac had to commit to conditioning after entering pro ball. Similarly, Bailey has tremendous raw power, though there’s work to be done for him to tap into it consistently. Some scouts feel he’s too stiff in the box and needs to change a setup that leads to swing-and-miss, while others do see some hit tool, but perhaps with a barrel that tends to be a bit late. Bailey’s surprising athleticism does give him the chance to be more than just a first baseman, though most feel that’s where he will eventually land. The Florida State recruit has seen time in left field and third base, where his above-average arm plays well. But it’s the power potential at the plate that could have teams interested in keeping the Tallahassee native from staying home for college, though some teams’ models will not like that he will be 19 when the Draft rolls around.

It’s a fairly regular occurrence for some high school bats from the Mid-Atlantic states to pop up as the Draft approaches. Jackson Merrill, a first-rounder in 2021 from Maryland is the big name, while Jonny Farmelo (2023) and Griffin Burkholder (2024) were Virginia products who went in the top two rounds of their Drafts. In some ways, Yow is ahead of his predecessors because none of that trio landed on MLB.com’s December Draft Top 100. It’s still hard to pinpoint where the Virginia prep shortstop fits because he didn’t do much on the summer showcase circuit, though he certainly opened eyes in Jupiter, Fla., this fall at Perfect Game’s WWBA World Championship. All conversations about Yow start with his speed. He might be the fastest player in the class, a true 80 runner, one who some scouts clocked doing a 6.15 60-yard dash at the Border Battle this fall. But while he has a slight build, he’s a super-twitchy athlete with some projection, he makes a ton of contact and he gets to some impact, even with a wood bat in his hands. He may never be a slugger, but no one predicted Trea Turner would hit 20-plus homers in the big leagues, either. That’s relevant because Yow does give off some Turner vibes. Like Turner from his amateur days, scouts aren’t sure if Yow and his average arm can stick at shortstop long-term (Turner has played over 1,100 games at the position), so teams might not want to look away from him at the premium position. After his pop-up performance in Jupiter, Yow decommitted from Richmond and signed on with Virginia for college in his Charlottesville backyard.

One of the smallest and least projectable prep pitchers in MLB Pipeline's Draft rankings, Sullivan also has one of the quickest arms and most explosive fastballs. He ran his heater up to 97 while dominating at the Area Code Games, though he struggled at the U.S. 18-and-under national team trials. He also has a pair of promising secondary offerings and his total package could land him a seven-figure bonus. Sullivan's fastball sat at 94-95 mph on the showcase circuit and has parked at 92-94 in the colder Ohio weather this spring, and its carry makes it difficult to hit and to command. His low-80s curveball with downer break shows the potential to become at least a solid weapon, as does his mid-80s changeup with fade and sink. He also has a short mid-80s slider. Sullivan has so much action on his pitches and some effort in his delivery that he sometimes struggles to find the strike zone. His quality athleticism eventually could translate into at least average control, though some scouts wonder if his lack of physicality or smooth mechanics will make it tough to hold up as a starter. Similarly built Jacob Miller hasn't lived up to expectations since the Marlins made him a supplemental first-round pick out of an Ohio high school in 2022, but he also didn't have Sullivan's power. A Tennessee commit, he'll be Draft-eligible as a sophomore in 2028 if he makes it to college.

Yes, it is that Bonds. Peyton is the son of Bobby Jr., who played 11 years of pro ball with the Padres, Giants and in indy ball, grandson of Bobby, whose big league career spanned 14 years, and nephew of Barry. Also an outfielder, Peyton Bonds went from Franklin HS in New Jersey -- where he was a teammate of A's prospect Joshua Kuroda-Grauer -- to Campbell University for his freshman year. He then returned to the Garden State to play for Rutgers, where he had a solid sophomore season, then turned his performance up a notch this spring, though a hamstring injury suffered in an April series against UCLA kept him off the field for a spell. At 6-foot-5, 230 pounds, Bonds looks like he was sent down from central casting, even if his current offensive profile doesn't quite fit the body type. He has a really good feel to hit, with excellent in-zone bat-to-ball skills. There's plenty of bat speed and high exit velocities, but it hasn't translated to power just yet, with some thinking there could be more unlocked with some bat path adjustments at the next level. While Bonds has average speed, maybe a tick better, he might not be a pure base stealer. But he can really play center field, with outstanding instincts to stay up the middle for a long time. He gets high marks for his plus makeup and passion for the game, perhaps handed down from his father, who grinded it out in the Minors for more than a decade.
