A two-way star in high school whose future is on the mound, Willoughby scored the game-winning run in extra innings in the Kentucky state championship game last June before performing well on the showcase circuit. He's a projectable athlete with the potential for three solid or better pitches once he's fully developed. A Kentucky commit, he'd be eligible for the Draft as a 21-year-old sophomore in 2028. Willoughby's fastball sits at 93-95 mph and tops out at 97 with armside run in short stints, though he works more in the low 90s when he ventures deeper into games. He displays advanced feel for a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink, and his cambio could become a plus pitch. He trusts it more than an upper-70s slider that features promising sweep but needs more power. Willoughby has a clean three-quarters delivery that translates into strikes with all three of his offerings. He already can spot his fastball to both sides of the plate and should add more velocity as he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame. He might blossom into a mid-rotation starter if he can refine a harder, more reliable slider.

Gallaher has established himself as one of the most clutch playoff performers in college baseball, earning MVP honors at NCAA regionals in each of his first two seasons while leading North Carolina to the Men's College World Series in 2024 and a victory shy of a return last June. Though he was the Tar Heels' best hitter as a sophomore, he hasn't performed as well this spring and scouts aren't quite sure what to make of him. He has slugged just .316 with two homers in 52 games during two summers with wood bats in the Cape Cod League, which hurts his cause. A right-handed hitter, Gallaher doesn't have any obvious weaknesses at the plate. He manages the strike zone well enough, shows the ability to handle lefties and righties and all types of pitches and makes hard flyball contact from gap to gap. His lack of power with wood is a concern, especially with a player who may not be able to handle a challenging defensive position. A below-average runner with average arm strength, Gallaher manned third base in his first two college seasons but the game sped up on him too much there. UNC shifted him to second base this year and he has played better than scouts expected. Some still question whether he has the actions and quickness to man the keystone in pro ball, so he could wind up in left field.

Scouts have been trying to figure out Vigue since his days as Massachusetts high schooler, when he could be unhittable at times and unable to find the strike zone others. That pattern continued in two years at Michigan, where he went undrafted as a sophomore-eligible in 2025. After switching schools, he has had an up-and-down season as Georgia's No. 2 starter and missed a turn in the rotation in late April with forearm tightness. Vigue gets more horizontal separation between his fastball and slider than almost any pitcher in the college crop. His 93-95 mph sinker reaches 98 with significant armside run, while his mid-80s slider has huge sweep in the opposite direction. He has utilized those two offerings 95 percent of the time this spring, rarely using a low-90s cutter and upper-80s changeup. Vigue generates plenty of swings and misses with his slider and weak contact with his fastball, but he has great difficulty landing either pitch in the zone on a regular basis. He rarely works past five innings, running up high pitch counts when hitters lay off his slider or he can't command his sinker. He has a strong 6-foot-3, 230-pound frame and a delivery that should provide more strikes, giving hope that he can add a third pitch and succeed as a starter in pro ball, but realistically he's more of a reliever.

Jorvorskie Lane Sr. rushed for a Texas A&M-record 49 touchdowns before spending three seasons in the National Football League. His son punishes baseballs rather than linebackers and is one of the more intriguing athletes and youngest players in the 2026 prep class. He projected as a first-round pick and drew Andrew McCutchen comps earlier in his high school career, though struggles during the summer and his senior season have dropped his stock. Lane has the potential for four solid-or-better tools but the key to his success will be the fifth. He creates impressive bat speed and raw power but his right-handed swing gets too long and uphill. He has difficulty making contact against quality pitching and does little damage when he doing so. Lane features plus speed and some evaluators give him the same grades for his arm and center-field play. There are some mixed reviews about his defense and thoughts that the Arkansas recruit may wind up on an outfield corner. He has also seen time at catcher and in the middle infield.

A .347/.465/.614 career hitter in two years at Maryland before transferring to Texas A&M for his draft spring, Hacopian has a ridiculous TrackMan readout (95% contact rate versus fastballs in 2025, including on Cape Cod, 57% hard-hit rate during his sophomore season with the Terps). He is less toolsy to the eye, however, as his kind of odd, high-effort swing, medium frame, and realistic 2B/3B fit on defense make him look more like a contact-oriented utilityman. Hacopian didn't really hit for power with wood on Cape Cod (he slugged .364), which is more in line with the expectations set by his look as a hitter (middling size, strength and a lot of effort needed to swing hard). He has more of a late-second or third round feel from a visual scouting standpoint, but might be someone's data darling.

Doyle is a freak. He generates incredible power with his lower body, and breaks the sound barrier when his torso follows his hips and unleashes a hellish upper-90s fastball toward the top of the strike zone. After he worked about 55 innings at Coastal Carolina and Ole Miss the last couple of years, Doyle held upper-90s gas throughout 95 frames in 2025. He threw his fastball for strikes at a 68% clip, which surprised me given how effortful and violent his delivery can look. But his season-long stamina, his repertoire depth, and his ability to land each pitch for strikes at an acceptable level gives him lots of starter traits in addition to the best pure stuff in the draft. Doyle's fastball has huge ride in the 95-97 mph range, will touch 100, and had a 40% miss rate in 2025. That's an elite fastball. 
His coffer of secondary pitches is led by a low-80s slider that you might as well call a slurve. It has tight, two-planed break (mostly lateral) that freezes hitters. Righties give up on it and lefties can't see it as it bends from the batter's box to the plate. His cutter is harder, 86-87 mph, but looks similar, and also has a stymying effect on hitters. His changeup feel is surprisingly good, and though it doesn't have huge movement, when hitters are geared up to try to catch 97 with ride, they're early. 
Doyle became a more complete pitcher throughout the season. Early on, he was leaning on his fastball 70% of the time. From May onward, his usage was much more balanced across his entire repertoire. Given his developmental context - multiple schools, in the bullpen a bunch as an underclassman - this is impressive. He is much more physical and athletically powerful than the other top-of-the-class pitchers and does stuff that, were you to see it on a big league field, would make your eyes pop out of your head. This is a freaky high-impact starter who is much closer to being ready than he was in February. Extrapolate on that if you want. He should go in the top two picks.

Famous and touted for about as long as it's possible for a high school prospect to be so, Holliday has been viewed as a top-of-the-draft candidate since teams were scouting his older brother a few years ago. Even though Jackson went first in that draft, sometimes scouts were leaving the boys' high school field more impressed with the bigger, stronger Ethan, who has the biggest power-hitting ceiling of any 2025 draft prospect. Holliday is incredibly physical and strong, and is an explosive rotator, absolutely electric for a guy his size; his swing has huge finish in the dirt behind him and natural lift toward the oppo gap. He has plus big league raw power right now and still has room for strength on his gigantic frame; the potential for top-of-the-scale raw power exists here. 
There are, however, also some alarming, pause-giving indicators related to Holliday's hit tool and ability to tap into all that power. He is very often late getting to pitches on the outer third of the zone. His swing is long and makes it tough for Holliday to pull fastballs at all, which is a red flag against high school heaters. He struck out a lot on the showcase circuit, posting a sub-70% contact with more whiffs than balls in play combined in 2023 and 2024, an 850-pitch sample. Despite his raw power, Ethan also didn't slug on the showcase circuit. Per Synergy, Holliday hit .246/.446/.346 combined in 2023 and 2024 against his most talented peers, not exactly the slash line of a windmill slam first overall pick. Teams confident they can adjust Holliday's swing to better keep him on time and help him get to his raw power should draft him with confidence at whatever pick, no matter how high. If you don't have a notion as to how you might accomplish that, you're playing with fire. 
Holliday is likely to play third base at the big league level and will need to mash to be an impact player.  At his present size, he is on the edge of what is typical/viable at shortstop, and he likely isn't done growing. He played a lot of third with Team USA, and his performance there was a mixed bag. He's a smooth, graceful defender who bends well for his size and has above-average feet, but below-average range and hands. Still, he's new to the position, and should be fine there with reps. This is rare raw power for a lefty-hitting infielder, but Holliday's swing-and-miss issues and a future corner fit on defense create risk. When you factor in the high-end outcomes for a guy like this, he's still an exciting, near top-of-the-class prospect who goes in the top three of most drafts.

Anderson is an eligible sophomore who threw just 38 innings as a freshman but showed exciting strikeout stuff. In 2025, he had a little velo bump, worked 119 frames, and led the entire country in strikeouts (180). Now he's a threat to go first in the draft. Anderson is a spindly 6-foot-2 lefty who'll show you four plus pitches. His fastball sits 92-94 with vertical ride and plays up because Anderson's loose arm action hides it until the very last moment. It generated a whopping 35% miss rate in 2025. The way his fastball plays means Anderson's command of it doesn't have to be precise; it rides enough to evade barrels in the strike zone. His slider, a mid-80s offering with big two-planed wipe, is often a pitch he goes to when he needs a strike, and he threw it for strikes at a 70% clip this year. His curveball and changeup usage doesn't exceed that of his slider, even against right-handed hitters. That might change in pro ball, as Anderson's changeup (which he sells with his whip-cracking arm speed) has enough late action to miss bats, and his curveball has lovely downward trajectory and depth that should make it a platoon neutralizer. He can also dump the curveball in the zone for strikes. Anderson is definitely a "control over command" type; he doesn't have great touch and feel for surgical location, he's a power pitcher. His stuff plays like a power pitcher's stuff. He doesn't have ideal size like Paul Skenes, who looks like he eats 200 innings for breakfast; he's skinnier and has just the one year of being stretched out like this, though his stuff was crisp late in the season. This is a fast-moving mid-rotation starter who has the toolkit to get just about anyone out.

Arquette transferred to Oregon State after a big sophomore year at Washington. He mostly played second base as a sophomore, then became the Beavers' shortstop. He entered the spring of 2025 as an anticipatory fit at short thanks to crafty actions and impressive body control for his size, and that turned out to be true. Arquette does play with a high center of gravity, and it's rare for athletes his size to be viable long-term shortstops, but his lightning quick exchange and plus arm help make up for mediocre range and bend. His struggles with grounders to his backhand, which pro teams will likely try to hide by positioning Arquette more toward third base. 
Arquette has exciting offensive upside for a shortstop because of his present power and long-term power projection. At 6-foot-5, 220 pounds, he's already comfortably larger than Corey Seager and Carlos Correa. Arquette's forearms are still pretty skinny and there are probably ways he can get even stronger in pro ball. This is a key area, as added strength might enable Arquette to shorten up and be a more complete hitter. His lever length and size can sometimes lead to awkward swings, and he has some vulnerability to elevated fastballs. He made roughly an average rate of contact (on the big league scale) against college pitching in 2025, which would lead one to believe it will be below average versus big league-quality stuff unless there are adjustments made as Arquette climbs. With as much power as he has (Arquette had one of the top hard-hit rates in all of college baseball at 58%, three standard deviations above the mean) and projects to have at peak (we're talking plus power now and 70-grade pop at maturity), it's going to be okay if he strikes out, so long as he stays at shortstop. This is easily the college hitter with the most upside in this draft.

Reclassified from the 2026 class, will be comfortably shy of 18 on draft day. Electric shortstop actions. Lightning-fast transfer with plus range. Arm strength should be sufficient for shortstop at physical maturity. Premium contact performance on the showcase circuit. Visual evaluation of Willits' feel to hit is not as exceptional as his numbers, but is still pretty strong. Swing is not always well-connected; puts the ball in play a ton, but it's not often scorched. Medium frame; power projection is modest. Higher-floored contact-oriented middle infielder whose power ceiling will depend on how much strength he can layer onto a medium frame.

Witherspoon spent his freshman season at Northwest Florida State before transferring to Oklahoma. He was walk-prone in 80 innings during sophomore year. His delivery last summer with Team USA was much more controlled and starter-like than what it was last spring at OU, and that carried over in to 2025, as Witherspoon walked just 6% of opponents. This is a tightly wound athlete with a short, deceptive, vertical arm stroke that appears out of nowhere from behind Witherspoon's head on release; he bears some mechanical similarities to Dylan Cease and Mark Melancon. He has a downhill mid-90s fastball with enough carry to play at the top of the zone when located, though it's more vulnerable the lower it lands. He works a cutter and slider off of that to different levels of his glove side; both have roughly the same shape, but the cutter is 88-91 while the slider is 84-88 and has a little more time to break. Witherspoon locates both of those pitches consistently to his glove side. His changeup and curveball are not as consistent but arguably the nastiest of his pitches when they're executed properly. His power upper-70s vertical curveball has identifiable pop out of Witherspoon's hand when he tries to dump it into the zone, but huge, hitter-pantsing finish when it's buried in the dirt. A power upper-80s changeup has bat-missing ability when located, though it's often too far from the zone to garner swings. Both the cambio and curveball were thrown for strikes at a 55% rate in 2025. Witherspoon entered the spring with relief risk, but he's quelled that. He still has some things to polish but he looks like a good team's no. 4 starter, with a powerful brand of athleticism helping drive his anticipated durability, and his initial small school dalliance giving one reason to believe there's more pitchability growth left in the tank.

Bremner was back and forth between the rotation and bullpen as an underclassman and dealt with periods of suppressed stuff and performance in 2025. He never really checked the "durability" box, as his 88 innings in 2024 were a career high, but at the end of his Gauchos career, Bremner had outstanding peripherals in all three seasons, he throws starter-quality strikes, has a starter's build, and his changeup is one of the best pitches in the whole draft. 
Bremner sits in the mid-90s with sink, but he tends to target the top of the strike zone anyway, and his heater missed bats at a rate similar to Kade Anderson's in 2025. His changeup has Bugs Bunny sink; it falls off the table in an almost supernatural way and is a plus-plus weapon that plays against lefties and righties alike. Bremner can toy with the top of the strike zone with his fastball and changeup the same way Chase Burns and Justin Verlander do with their fastball and a breaking ball. Good luck guessing which pitch it is and where it will finish. Bremner's slider needs consistency. It has average length at above-average velocities, but its shape and location are all over he place. Sometimes it breaks straight down, others it has typical slider two-plane direction, and too often it backs up on him. There might be relatively simple tweaks that can be made to his stride direction that help unlock better fastball shape and a more enticing slider angle and location. It doesn't feel like Bremner is done developing and the raw material for him to be a good mid-rotation starter is still here, even though he didn't put it all together in 2025. He should still come off the board in the top 10.

Bremner was back and forth between the rotation and bullpen as an underclassman and dealt with periods of suppressed stuff and performance in 2025. He never really checked the "durability" box, as his 88 innings in 2024 were a career high, but at the end of his Gauchos career, Bremner had outstanding peripherals in all three seasons, he throws starter-quality strikes, has a starter's build, and his changeup is one of the best pitches in the whole draft. 
Bremner sits in the mid-90s with sink, but he tends to target the top of the strike zone anyway, and his heater missed bats at a rate similar to Kade Anderson's in 2025. His changeup has Bugs Bunny sink; it falls off the table in an almost supernatural way and is a plus-plus weapon that plays against lefties and righties alike. Bremner can toy with the top of the strike zone with his fastball and changeup the same way Chase Burns and Justin Verlander do with their fastball and a breaking ball. Good luck guessing which pitch it is and where it will finish. Bremner's slider needs consistency. It has average length at above-average velocities, but its shape and location are all over he place. Sometimes it breaks straight down, others it has typical slider two-plane direction, and too often it backs up on him. There might be relatively simple tweaks that can be made to his stride direction that help unlock better fastball shape and a more enticing slider angle and location. It doesn't feel like Bremner is done developing and the raw material for him to be a good mid-rotation starter is still here, even though he didn't put it all together in 2025. He should still come off the board in the top 10.

Cunningham is a squat-bodied middle infielder with well-below-average physical projection, but he's also arguably the best pure hitter in the draft regardless of demographic. He has explosive hands, quick enough to snatch fastballs at the top of the zone, and is adept at adjusting the posture of both his upper and lower body to move the barrel all over the place. Cunningham has very special feel to hit and surprising power for his size. He has surprising speed, too; he ran some 4.15s and 4.4s with the turn last summer. It's tough to find a body comp here, but Alex Bregman is close and also sets some amount of precedent for an athlete this size turning into a great hitter. Limited arm strength relegates Cunningham to second base, so he has to rake to be an impact player, but he's never done anything but that.

A sensational athlete with an ideal pitcher's frame, Hernandez has monster arm strength and potentially huge secondary stuff. He often sits in the mid-to-upper-90s and will touch 100. Hernandez has a strapping 6-foot-4 QB frame with room for more strength. He also has ridiculous arm speed. His fastball is frustratingly vulnerable due to inconsistent movement and location; the former needs to be ironed out proactively upon entry to pro ball. His pronator-style changeup has huge tailing action and plus-plus potential thanks to Hernandez's arm speed. The slider is less consistent and vulnerable when it isn't good; it's mostly 82-85 with two-plane wipe, but the best ones are plus. Hernandez takes a great BP and makes some amazing plays at first base, which is evidence that he's an outstanding athlete who one can expect to make adjustments on the mound. This is a huge-ceiling high school pitcher who will likely be the first one off the board in 2025. He could go inside the draft's top 10.

Irish has been a steady, three-year SEC performer culminating in a .364/.469/.710 junior year line. During his two underclass seasons, Irish played a mix of catcher, first base, and a little bit of right field. Whether or not he could actually catch was a big point of contention entering the season, and we didn't really get to find out. Irish was hit by a pitch in March that fractured his right scapula, and he mostly played the outfield the rest of the season. My underclass notes on his catching: Will pop close to 1.90 but often fumbles his exchange, fair receiver and pitch framer, but not a good ball-blocker right now. Irish's arm in the outfield is sensational, and he'll be able to play right (his feel for the outfield is predictably raw; he needs reps out there) if it turns out he can't catch, but it makes sense that whatever teams are highest on him are probably so because they think he might stay behind the plate. 
Irish is a solid average contact hitter and has plus power. He's especially good at flattening his swing to snatch elevated fastballs, though because he's hunting these pitches, he has a tendency to expand the zone against high heaters. He shows some ability to dip into his lower half to at least spoil lower pitches, but Irish tends to smash them into the ground. Pro opponents might be happy to have him hit hard grounders into play and just live toward the bottom of the zone against him. Irish has everyday upside as a catcher and looks more like a good platoon bat were he to settle into right field.

Aloy transferred from Sacramento State to Arkansas after his freshman year with the Hornets. His offensive production took a bit of a hit (from a 1.089 OPS to .841), but then he crushed on Cape Cod (where he hit eight homers in 21 games) and as a junior (he won SEC Player of the Year with a .350/.434/.673 line and 21 bombs). Aside from a concerning amount of chase, Aloy does at least a little bit of everything. He's a plus athlete with an athletic build, plus arm, above-average range, and average hands. He struggles some with hot shots, but otherwise looks like a pretty clean shortstop fit. Aloy also has plus bat speed and power to all fields. He had one of the best hard-hit rates (58%) in college baseball last year, and he's a threat to go deep from pole to pole, which he's demonstrated with wood bats. It takes big effort and it comes at a cost: strikeouts. 
Aloy made a slightly below-average amount of contact in 2024, but an adjustment period from the WAC to the SEC felt natural. He entered 2025 as someone who I expected to make a leap from a bat-to-ball standpoint and solidify himself as one of the top couple of players in the draft, and while he won SEC PoY, that didn't happen in a statistical sense. Aloy chases a ton and doesn't track pitches especially well. His stride takes him to a precarious-looking toe tap, which seems hard to balance. This is the sort of athlete who looks like he could easily make mechanical adjustments that help him lean into his power, but he's probably always going to have elevated K rates because of chase. There's volatility here because of that, but Aloy's tools are really big.

Carlson is a slam dunk shortstop with a premium arm. His projectable frame, which is sinewy but strong already, has room for 15 or 20 pounds without compromising his athleticism. Carlson doesn't track pitches especially well but his contact rates on the showcase circuit (88% contact%, 15% chase) were very strong. He rotates well and swings hard, generating plus bat speed, and has some pull ability on the inner half despite his lever length. He has a scissor style stride, and not everyone loves this swing, which looks a lot like that of Twins prospect Rayne Doncon's and could be more vulnerable to pro fastballs than it has been in high school. Though he has some hit tool risk, Carlson presents an exciting combination of defensive impact, contact performance, and power projection, and is very likely a top 10 or so pick.

A South Dakota high schooler then two-way JUCO prospect at Iowa Western. Was in the Tennessee bullpen as a sophomore, then moved to the rotation in 2025. Had a great year in certain key ways (most notably stamina, stuff retention late in the season) and not in others (fastball command). Looks like an outside linebacker coming at you down the mound at roughly 6-foot-6, 250 pounds. Long, loose, if somewhat violent arm stroke, plus-plus extension, sits 96 and touches 101 from a near sidearm slot. Fastball cuts at times, tails at others. Paired with mid-to-upper 80s gyro slider that has hard late break. Ones with two-planed movement are plus, ones that move more laterally and less vertically are fringy. Throws strikes with both but not in great locations, and Phillips' fastball shape simply requires his locations be better. Minimal changeup usage at this point, little to no vert, above-average horizontal break. You can see he has feel for creating action on it, but not for locating it. Busted out some nasty right-on-right cambios against Arkansas in the postseason (ask Ryder Helfrick) but doesn't trust it yet. Body and athlete scream "starter," command and repertoire don't as of yet, but re-read the first two sentences of this report and project on this barely 21-year-old unit.

Explosive lefty power bat with a (somewhat small sample) contact performance that reinforces confidence in Parker's ability to access his power. Sweeping bat path similar to Walker Jenkins and Brady Ebel with dangerous low ball uppercut. Has shown some ability to flatten his swing to cover the top of the zone, with some oppo-poked contact of this style. Has worked out at shortstop, but a boxy frame and below-average mobility and hands will probably push him to third base and possibly the outfield. Good bend in lower body gives him a fair shot to stay on the infield. Has a little less bat-to-ball track record as the other elite prospects, but has the contact/power combo to be an everyday player.

Transferred from Louisville to Tennessee after two years with the Cardinals. Posted plus contact rates in both underclass seasons but overall line was still a little below average in each due to lack of power. Then had a monster junior year with an 1.100 OPS. Plus lefty contact bat with modest power. Really loose hitting hands, tracks pitches well and moves bat around the zone, best in the lower two thirds. Has doubles pop thanks to consistent contact quality, but is unlikely to hit 20-plus bombs. Improved look at shortstop as a junior, has a shot to be nearly average there. Makes the routine plays comfortably, but lacks a standout individual tool like plus range or arm strength. Would definitely be playing second base on a bunch of big league rosters, but in a vacuum could stand at shortstop. Among the higher-floored players in the 2025 draft, profiles as a second-division regular middle infielder.

One of the most consistently productive college hitters in this year's class. Finished his Indiana career with a .350/.459/.672 line, and raked with wood in two years of summer ball. Gorgeous feel for all-fields contact, can drive pitches on the outer third to the opposite field with power and turn on pitches on the inner half. Makes it look easy the way he reads and reacts to pitch location and speed. Can adjust hands and upper body posture to put the barrel on the ball. Lower launch guy who might not quite hit for his raw power in games. Terrible outfield defender; might just be a DH. Among the more stable hitters in the draft and a likely first round pick. Defensive piece is a body blow to his overall value and gives him basically zero margin for error as a hitter, but Taylor should do enough to, in essence, be an everyday bat.

Arnold is a funky, drop-and-drive low-slot southpaw with plus peak velocity and an uphill approach angle. He carried a 2.98 ERA across 105.2 IP in 2024, posting 159 strikeouts, and a 1.10 WHIP. His 2025 was not as dominant. Arnold's strike-throwing (especially with the fastball) backed up, and his FIP was nearly a full run higher than it was in 2024. Arnold is a super long-levered 6-foot-1 or so, but he generates 6-foot-4 extension with a deep, cross-bodied stride; his release height is a shade under four-and-a-half feet, with huge uphill angle. His arm stroke and slot are in the Madison Bumgarner area, and he boasts mechanical grace and fluidity commensurate with a starter. Arnold posted a plus-plus fastball CSW% in 2024; he sat in the low-to-mid-90s at FSU, then was more comfortably in the mid-90s during the summer of 2024 with Team USA. That pitch, and Arnold's feel for it, regressed significantly in 2025. It went from missing bats at a rate closer to Kade Anderson's fastball, to one doing so at an average level, and with a tick less velocity than last year. 
Arnold's slider bails him out when he falls behind tiwh the fastball. If you're a left-handed hitter, this is a Freddy Krueger slider. It starts in the middle of the lefty batter's box and finishes on the plate, or bends from the middle of the plate into the righty batter's box. Even as Arnold had to use it more to climb back into counts, this pitch played like a plus offering in terms of miss and chase. His changeup flashes bat-missing tail but is often nowhere near the zone, and Arnold has thrown what look like a few upper-80s cutters. Especially if his fastball problems persist, more frequent cutter usage might be in order. Though no longer a top-of-the-class prospect, Arnold should still come off the board around pick 10.

Well-rounded switch-hitting catcher with plus bat-to-ball ability from both sides of the plate. All-fields spray with low ball power as a lefty, more oppo-gap oriented as a righty. Posted a 93% zone contact rate as a sophomore and 96% as a junior; measurable power is a little south of the big league average but not by much. Late tip in hands (more pronounced from left side) might make him late on pro velo, but otherwise is a very stable prospect as a hitter. A bit of a project on defense. Receiving and ball-blocking Team USA stuff was a challenge for him in 2024. Became a better framer in 2025 as, per Synergy, 57% of borderline pitches were called strikes. Has a manic style on defense, and staccato style of receiving with quick, short movements. Ball-blocking is still a real problem for him. Throwing is above average, however; makes accurate throws from funky platforms when he has to. Contact-oriented primary catcher projection.

Triston "Murf" Gray - you might see him listed as either depending on where you're looking - is a mid-major performer who posted a 60-grade contact rate and 70-grade in-zone contact rate in 2024, and backed up those metrics on Cape Cod and as a junior. Physical, 6-foot-4 power hitter. Bucket strider who can still get extended and cover the outer edge of the zone. Has some chase issues and his swing can look atypical at times, but this is a fairly complete hitter on paper. Geared to pull, can adjust his posture and path enough to cover fastballs at the top of the strike zone. 91% contact versus fastballs in 2025. Size limits his mobility somewhat at third base but he moves well for his size and has plenty of arm. Below-average hands, struggles with hotshots. Mid-to-late first round for me due to power, performance track record and overt big league physicality.

Power-over-hit profile. Substantial swing-and-miss risk; ran a 71% contact rate combined in 2023 and 2024. Approaching plus power right now, with plus bat speed; swing features big leverage and loft. Strapping 6-foot-4 frame and is going to get stronger; plus-plus power projection. Could be a 30-grade contact hitter with 70-grade power, and it would be totally fine. Pitched and played a mix of corner positions on the showcase circuit. Arm strength makes him a potentially viable third baseman, but his size, potential lack of mobility, and below-average hands create corner outfield and first base risk. High-variance prospect with enough playable power to justify the dice roll in the middle of the first round.

Toured the American South throughout his college career, with stops at Duke, Ole Miss, and then finally Tennessee for his draft year, during which he slashed .341/.497/.760. Roster fit at Tennessee meant Fischer played more first base than third base by a wide margin. Played mostly third at Ole Miss, also has experience at second and in left. Looked fine enough at third in 2024 to merit pro development there. Range and arm are a fit there, hands need polish. Big uppercut swing, averaged 18 degrees of launch in 2025. Medium-framed with powerful arms generating big leverage through effort and strength. More about consistent hard contact with lift rather than enormous top-end raw power. Apt to swing over softer stuff, even when it doesn't quite finish below the zone. Middle range outcome is that of a valuable corner platoon bat, ultimate upside is an everyday player.

LaViolette entered his draft spring as a career .297/.433/.683 hitter with 50 homers in two seasons at A&M, then flopped as a junior. He posted a contact rate (69%), much worse than just one standard deviation below the college average. LaViolette's body seemed bigger, stiffer, and less explosive. He wasn't tracking pitches well and was just mashing mistakes in the middle of the plate; his measureable power took a dip as a junior, too. One could be inclined to regress LaViolette's performance to his career mean, and weigh more heavily his two prior years of performance, as if his junior year is an anomaly and not the start of a declining trend in ability. But he sure looked like he had backed up; it wasn't just a tough luck year for him in a BABIP sense or something like that, he was clearly worse. He might be someone's buy-low target in the mid-to-late first round, but based on how he looked all year, this was a real change and dip in talent and I wouldn't bite until later in round two. LaViolette has to be taken with preconceived notions about how to get him back to peak form; it doesn't seem likely to happen on its own.

LaViolette has to be taken with preconceived notions about how to get him back to peak form; it doesn't seem likely to happen on its own.

Presents kind of a lefty Coby Mayo look. Huge-framed high school hitter with big physical projection. Tightly wound athlete, especially in the lower body. Awkward throwing stroke. Worked out on the infield but projects to move to the outfield in pro ball. Generates impressive power in a short mechanical distance. Produced 87% contact rate on the showcase circuit, but the sample was smaller than some of his peers. Strong top hand through contact, has power to oppo gap and to pull side. Shot to be an everyday corner guy if the contact piece of the profile is real.

Wood was a power reliever during his first two years in Fayetteville and then moved into the rotation as a junior, only to be shut down pretty quickly with a shoulder injury that limited him to 10 starts and 37 regular season innings. To say Wood looked healthy when he returned would be an understatement. At the College World Series, Gage did his best Kerry Wood impression and ripped riding fastballs and knee-buckling curveballs past Murray State hitters in a 19-strikeout no-hitter. 
Wood is small, he's now had injury issues, and he really only has two pitches at the moment, and yet he still might go in the middle of the first round because his fastball's velo/ride/angle cocktail is deadly, and his curveball's vertical snap plays beautifully off of it. Are there echoes of Ty Floyd here? That's not going great. Wood is similar in stature and repertoire. His ability to spin the baseball should yield at least one other good breaking ball. He threw something like 50 cutter/sliders and 15 changeups in all of 2025; those pitches are raw. Adding to Wood's relief risk is that he can only consistently throw his fastball for strikes, but even that is a developmental win considering he was in the bullpen a year ago, and recall that there are many big league starters who feast off of heavy fastball usage when it rides like Wood's does. He's risky but could be a good no. 4 starter.

Athletic, well-conditioned, smedium-framed lefty with deceptive arm stroke. Fastball played like a comfortably plus pitch despite below-average velocity because Thompson's mechanics hide the ball so well and generate uphill angle with vertical ride on his heater. Most-used secondary in 2024 was a mid-70s curveball, but incorporated a low-80s slider in 2025. Pitches have five ticks of separation on average, but blend together around the 80 mph mark. Vertical arm stroke helps add depth to both, which are more commonly located in the zone than for chase. Thompson's changeup shows some of the classic markers of a vert slot guy; it's tough to turn over consistently. Many of them sail on him, but he can occasionally create enough tailing action to miss bats. His rate stats on the changeup in 2025 were promising in terms of miss and chase but some of that is because so few of them were in the zone that any swing was chasing it. Threw starter-quality strikes as a sophomore and junior, worked 90 innings in 2025. Pretty stable starter prospect with chance for four viable pitches. Fastball will (literally) carry him.

Exciting shortstop defender with plus contact skills. Average range, plays up due to body control and ability to make acrobatic throws. A virtual lock to stay at short, has a chance to be plus there. Plus contact and below-average power combo on offense. Passive hitter who often takes strikes right down the middle. All-fields contact spray, tracks pitches well, moves the barrel all over the zone, cuts stride with two strikes. Swing has an abbreviated finish, produces doubles contact. Limited power ceiling, but a high-probability low-end everyday shortstop thanks to contact and defense.

Spent two years at College of the Canyons prior to junior year as an Anteater. Slashed .336/.447/.591, underlying metrics about average while power is below. Gap-to-gap fastball hitter, in limited sample of pitched 93 mph and above (92 pitches) had a 77% contact rate and slugged .700. Narrowly-built 6-foot-2, looks small on the field but his measurables are more typical for a big leaguer. Might add meaningful power on a pro strength program. Slam dunk shortstop with plus arm. Makes everything look easy on defense. Plus-plus hands, plus range, incredible ability to flip his hips and rocket one over to first. Defense gives him a strong utility infield floor, bat has some upside depending on how Yeoman's physicality trends into his 20s.

Hit .389/.467/.704 during his sophomore year at Marist, .385/.433/.486 on Cape Cod, then transferred to Wake for his draft year, which was cut short by a left shoulder injury and surgery. Performed well during the month that he played, evident on the surface and in his underlying data. Has a classic lefty uppercut swing but is still able to cover the top of the strike zone pretty well. Fluid rotator with above-average bat speed. Struggled some to identify breaking balls at Marist; there's some hit tool volatility here just because Conrad is coming out of a smaller program (we had barely gotten into conference play when he got hurt) and might require an adjustment period against better stuff. Played a mix of outfield and first base at Marist; then played center field at Wake. Runs well enough to try center field in pro ball; he didn't look amazing out there, but he's barely played it. Looked like a middle-of-the-first-round guy prior to the injury.

Defensive wizard with low-ball power. Has made several ludicrous, game-altering defensive plays in center field. Plus runner and athlete who's fearless around the wall and warning track. Profile has a high floor because of the defense. Hit tool risk on offense. Loads with an arm bar; cut is too long to time a lot of fastballs on the outer half. Timing at the dish comes and goes. Authoritative hands, sprays balls all around the diamond with power. Slight frame, has been skinny forever and might not ever have typical big league strength. Right labrum surgery in 2024 may have impacted his offensive output in 2025, as Cannarella's power output dipped. Still a good prospect because of his defense, which gives him a floor as a good fourth outfielder.

Generates incredible arm speed, with as loose and whippy an arm action as there is in the class. Huge hop down the mound, big extension with the potential for nasty uphill movement. Fastball tends to sink and tail right now. Two-planed, sweeper-shaped slider in the upper 70s, projects to plus. Would piece together nicely with a more consistent four-seam version of Cervantes' fastball; he'll likely have both two- and four-seam versions at maturity. Tailing, plus-flashing changeup in the low-80s. Got in better shape and velo took a leap this spring, up to 97. Big-ceiling'd pitching prospect with great fastball/breaker foundation.

Broad-shouldered 6-foot-5 pitcher's frame with lots of room for strength without altering mobility. Fastball features explosive rise/run life when located to the correct part of the zone and above. Was routinely 94-97 mph late in the summer and fall of 2024, peaking at 98 in the spring and sitting more 93-95. Showed upper-70s breaking ball with shape that fits nicely with the rise/run nature of his heater, added power to it as a senior and it was 83-85 mph. No changeup feel, arm action is long and potentially a second bit of low-hanging fruit for dev. Secondary stuff requires more projection than most exciting high schoolers, but the ceiling on Harmon's fastball is enormous, and the paths to developing his secondary stuff are well tread throughout the league.

In line with the Owen Murphy-type prep arms, bigger-bodied dude but really limber and athletic. Gorgeous arm action with vertical fastball/breaking ball combo. Fastball was more 88-92 last summer, then 92-95 this spring with 2,500 rpm and 17 inches IVB on average. Natural supinator with big two-planed curveball in the 78-82 mph range, 2,900 rpm. Fastball has natural cut at times and Fisher might have an explicit cutter at maturity. Foundation to be able to add multiple breaking balls and maybe a kick change is here. Pretty typical comp round pitching prospect.

Draft-eligible sophomore who crushed during his two years at UVA and is now committed to Tennessee via the transfer portal and not expected to sign. Well-built 6-foot-5, 200 pound guy with corner infield experience. Moved from first base to right field in 2025 and is currently playing center field on Cape Cod. Lever length and late-triggering hands create an inside-out nature to ball-in-play profile; much more apt to pull breaking balls with authority than fastballs. Has explosive hands and bat speed, some feel to hit, and power that's already shown up in game action. Has below-average plate discipline, but the tools and projection foundation here is exciting and features a lot of power now, and probably more in the future. A first round prospect entering 2026.

One of the toughest evals of this draft class. Destroyed on the showcase circuit despite an odd-looking swing. Incredibly short and closed-off stride in the box, very upright throughout his operation; think Giancarlo Stanton's swing if he kept his feet closer together. Will this make it impossible for Fien to dip and scoop low pitches in pro ball? Showed some ability to drop the bat head to get to them on the showcase circuit, then really struggled during his senior spring. Authoritative top hand through contact, flattens out to cover belt-high pitches with power. Not a lock to stay on the infield. Plays with high center of gravity, scattered throwing accuracy. Arm looks awesome from the outfield when Fien can put his entire body into each bolt. Could be a plus right fielder with a plus arm. Looked lean and lithe enough as a rising junior to put center field in his mix, but added mass as a senior makes that more of a pipe dream. This eval is likely below the industry consensus due to my instincts around the viability of Fien's swing.

Elite speedster who turns 18 a couple weeks after the 2025 draft, one of the youngest players available. Reclassified from the 2026 grads late in the fall of 2024, and so was scouted with less focus during the summer of 2024 (when teams didn't know he'd be eligible) and more during the spring of 2025. Became much, much stronger throughout the summer of 2024; arms grew more than the Grinch's heart during that span. Contact performance in a relatively limited underclass showcase environment was only fair, breaking balls evaded him at a concerning rate. More catalyst than slugger, slash-and-dash style with oppo gap tendency. Breathtaking speed, one of the fastest players in the class. Reaches top speed in the blink of an eye, will post some 4.00 run times to first, looks like he's floating from bases to base, maintains top speed as he changes direction. This is game-changing speed even at the big league level. May not make much of an offensive impact beyond that aspect of his game, should be in the late first round mix à la Kellon Lindsey last year.

Super projectable shortstop and near lock to stay at the position. Silky smooth defender with plus body control. Impressive bend and hands for his size, arm stroke is short and consistent and produces strong, accurate throws right into the chest of the first baseman. More a long-term projection play on offense. Has feel for adjusting body posture to help mitigate lever length, but slow-twitch in-the-box athleticism puts him at risk of being habitually late. Comfortably below-average power right now, but frame has all kinds of projection. Less showcase track record than is typical for an elite prospect, but hit well in the little bit he participated in. Defense gives him a floor of sorts, offensive upside is dependent on Yost developing functional strength that can help him shorten up.

Lovely hitting hands. Has made a ton of contact across the last two calendar years. Has barrel feel and oppo ability on pitches away from him, and is frequently on time to pull the ball (though more often against softer stuff). Medium leg kick in terms of height, but big in terms of how long and slow it is. Lacks big bat speed and explosion. Rigid actions as a defender behind the plate, likely ends up in a corner outfield spot. 45 arm. Quality bat path from the left side of the plate but average at best bat speed through the zone. Flashes average raw power to the pull side. Worth keeping tabs on but more of a low variance corner bat driven by his hit tool.

Toolsy, body-beautiful outfielder who had a bit of a disappointing junior season with half as many homers (four) as during his sophomore year, and in a hitter-friendly park in Tucson to boot. Above-average runner with below-average feel for defense. Played center field as a sophomore but not as a junior. Ball skills are questionable but not so bad as to declare him a definite corner guy. Was a more explosive rotator in the batter's box as a soph. High, tapered waist, athletic lower half through contact. Swing looks fairly short for his size, but Summerhill tends to be late on fastballs and struggles to pull them. Hit for doubles power as a sophomore with 87% contact rate, and entered junior year with a shot to move into the back of the first round, but still feels more like a second rounder for teams willing to overlook some off-field issues and buy low on him, performance-wise.

Superlative size and arm strength, massive power projection, very poor hit tool performance on the showcase circuit with more whiffs than balls in play. Lever length makes it tough for him to be on time; impact contact comes in a fairly narrow part of the strike zone. Range and bend on defense is surprisingly good considering Young's size. Has multi-positional potential as 3B/RF and has the athleticism to be proficient at both. Comes from a family of great big leaguers (Dmitri, Delmon) and is an exciting prospect because of his power potential, but Young swung and missed so much against his elite peers that one has to be apprehensive about his ability to tap into that power.

Freaky switch-hitting catcher with plus present power and enormous long-term power potential. Built like he's going to Oregon to play tight end rather than catcher at a long-levered 6-foot-4, 220 or so, with room for more strength without borrowing from his mobility. Didn't play much showcase circuit ball, blew up at Super 60 prior to the season, then had the most impressive Combine BP among high school players, putting balls out of Chase Field from both sides of the dish. It was a titanic, stock-altering showing in Phoenix. Lack of showcase performance and quality of Midwest high school play makes the hit tool piece of Gray's profile tough to project, and for the same reasons his long-term fit as a catcher is, too. High school catching is already a risky demo, but Gray's upside is seductive. Here he's in the early second round area.

Amazing grace and fluidity for his size, plays the game low to the ground for a 6-foot-8 guy. Coasting with quality fastball strikes at 91-94, touched 96 at Area Codes, sat 95-97 in the PG All-American game, then was more 92-94 for starts the following spring. Secondary stuff is not especially nasty right now. Would go entire high school starts without throwing his breaking ball. Changeup has power sink and could be plus at peak, advanced feel for location, can lean on it when he's behind in the count. Goes through periods where his four-seamer is sailing on him and he shifts to two-seamers within a start to get the pitch to sit down in the zone. It worked against high schoolers due to sheer velo but might not be a viable crutch against pro hitters. Plus command and durability projection, love the size, athleticism (have you ever seen a 6-foot-8 kid execute a perfect pop-up at the end of a hustle double?) and ease of operation, but it might be tough to meet a rumored $3 million ask when the player in question lacks a good breaker.

Patient speedster with advanced bat control. Had a .616 OBP on the showcase circuit because of his plate discipline, contact ability, and speed. Can really bend into his lower half to adjust barrel depth. Average bat speed, not especially explosive or projectable. Can really run, should be center field fit even though his feel for defense is just okay. Lack of arm strength would shift him to left field if his reads remain inconsistent. If his secondary skills hold water all the way through the minors, de Brun could be Brandon Nimmo type of player.

Sinewy, projectable, left-handed hitting infielder with natural uppercut bat path. Swings bent at waist, creating vertical path throughout the hitting zone. Exciting hip and hand separation, body is well-connected throughout his swing and all that energy eventually leaves through his hands. Can move the barrel around. Best at scooping low pitches, but also shows some ability to flatten and cover around the belt. Does not track pitches well, however. Head doesn't stay on the ball, swung through a lot of in-zone fastballs in a limited showcase sample. Pitched and played shortstop at his high school, but was relegated to lesser positions with Team USA. Has a relatively odd throwing stroke and is a near sidearm slot on the mound. Not a lock to stay at short in pro ball, but should be sent out there to see whether or not the throwing style plays. Exciting power-hitting potential because of the loft in Owens' swing, other aspects of his game are mixed.

Sinewy, projectable, left-handed hitting infielder with natural uppercut bat path. Swings bent at waist, creating vertical path throughout the hitting zone. Exciting hip and hand separation, body is well-connected throughout his swing and all that energy eventually leaves through his hands. Can move the barrel around. Best at scooping low pitches, but also shows some ability to flatten and cover around the belt. Does not track pitches well, however. Head doesn't stay on the ball, swung through a lot of in-zone fastballs in a limited showcase sample. Pitched and played shortstop at his high school, but was relegated to lesser positions with Team USA. Has a relatively odd throwing stroke and is a near sidearm slot on the mound. Not a lock to stay at short in pro ball, but should be sent out there to see whether or not the throwing style plays. Exciting power-hitting potential because of the loft in Owens' swing, other aspects of his game are mixed.

Tightly wound athlete who was a mixed bag on defense during his showcase summer. Plus straightline speed, range, and arm strength, but mixed accuracy. Web gems at some events, flubs at others. Has the athletic ability to fit at shortstop, just needs polish. Explosive move forward in the batter's box, stride encompasses most of the chalked area. Hands are explosive but noisy, and take a good bit of time to really get going. Struggles to pull the ball due to late barrel entry, lots of oppo contact when he's not entirely late on fastballs. Power-over-hit shortstop prospect graded in the early second round area.

Super long-levered infield prospect with extreme uphill swing. Already pretty strong for his age but has room for immense strength as he matures. If Becker can shorten up as he gets stronger then we might really have something here, but as of now, his swing is terrifyingly long. Some of that is lever length (this is a 6-foot-4 shortstop) and some is swing path. Geared for launch, bottom hand dominant, rotates well through contact. Unlike a lot of longer-levered hitters, there isn't an obvious hole in Becker's swing; most of his whiffs come off the plate. Legit shot to stay at shortstop despite his size. Bends well, has impressive lateral agility, often makes the field look small. Throwing stroke is a little odd, but I have no documented issues with accuracy. Might move off shortstop due to sheer size at maturity, but talent-wise he's a fit there. Power-hitting shortstop prospect with hit tool risk due to swing style.

Draft-eligible sophomore who slashed .284/.420/.535 as a freshman, then had a bit of a strikeout regression in 2025 (24% K). Combo of power (58% hard hit rate) and patience, but a grooved swing leads to well below-average contact. Can pull fastballs at the top of the zone, struggles with stuff down and away. Really struggles to dip and spoil changeups. Flexible, low-to-the ground pitch framer. Quiet at the catch point and even gets to mislocated pitches in time to make them look presentable. Ball-blocking hands are great, lateral agility is not. Struggles to push from left to right in his one-knee'd stance but great at picking balls in the dirt when they're in front of him. Raw arm strength is fair, but often takes entirely too long to get rid of the baseball, and often mishandles his exchange. Looked like potential mid-first rounder entering 2025 and leaves junior year more in round two.

Quick-handed second base-only prospect with middling power. Buttons fastballs as well as any college hitter and is usually on time to pull the ball; can turn on pitches tailing in around his hands à la Cody Ross. Had a 93-94% contact rate versus heaters each of the last two seasons. Should get to whatever power he has by virtue of contact talent and pull/lift ability, but doesn't have a ton of raw juice; had a 107 mph max exit velo in 2025. Below-average range at second base, but makes up for it with skillful and accurate throwing. Probably a second base-only fit on the infield, might explore outfield in pro ball to increase versatility since Godbout lacks the power of an everyday second baseman.

Began college career as a hitter but shifted to pitching full-time after he broke his hand in 2024. Was a low-slot power reliever initially, then moved into the rotation in 2025 and had a stellar season - 15 starts, 71.1 IP, 3.09 FIP, 37% K% - while pumping mid-to-upper-90s heat all spring. Short-striding low-slot guy with big-spinning fastball. Its shape isn't great, but the pitch has so much life that it plays anyway, and Forbes' low arm slot helps it have bat-missing utility at the belt. Nightmare pitch for indecisive right-handed hitters who'll check swing their wrists and elbows right into the path of Forbes' fastball. Bends low-80s sweeper to his glove side with shape mirroring that of his fastball. Big lateral wipe, plus offering. Only threw 62% fastball strikes and 58% slider strikes in 2025. Cutter and changeup are distant whispers at this point, barely a part of Forbes' repertoire. Limited toolkit and control signal big relief risk, but of course Forbes has a two-way background and was in the bullpen for two years, so he might have late skill projection.

Coming out of high school, had offers from Florida, Florida State, Ole Miss, Mississippi State and Auburn to play offensive line, but wanted to play baseball at 'Bama. Good decision, is about to go late first round-ish. Six-foot-six sinkerballer up to 99. Some of these sinkers have incredible tail and draw embarrassing swings from righties who nearly get hit by the pitch. Lower-effort delivery but doesn't repeat, lacks feel for consistent release. Scatters his entire repertoire; sharpening command will be biggest developmental priority in pro ball. Four-pitch mix. Changeup in the 86-90 mph range flashes plus and has right-on-right utility, slider and cutter give him glove-side weapons. Heavy slider usage against righties, only playing like an average pitch. Was coming off TJ in 2025, entered the season with 25 collegiate innings. Size and inexperience give Smith's profile exciting late-bloomer characteristics.

Big-framed long reliever who will likely be upcycled into a starter as a pro. Sat 96 from high-three-quarters slot. Cutter/slider combo is a nightmare in on the hands and knees of lefties, might have the tools to get lefties out even without a changeup. Feel for consistent glove-side location, but really only works to that half of the plate, which might have to change against pro hitters. Whether or not he has season-long starter stamina is a black box right now because he hasn't done it, so I'm sticking with long relief projection here because we at least know he can do that at a high level, but this guy should go out as a starter.

Born in Puerto Rico, went to high school in Florida and began his college career at UF as a two-way guy who barely played. Transferred to Pasco-Hernando State College in Florida for his second year, crushed the Northwoods League during the summer of 2024, and transferred to Virginia. Has a much higher ceiling as a hitter. Rare lefty power and power projection. Feel to hit is raw, but Arroyo has barely played and hasn't yet focused solely on hitting (he threw 12 innings in 2025). Slashed .291/.361/.519 with a 13.8 K% and 89% zone contact rate in 2025. Won't be 21 until September, lots of late-bloomer traits here.

After Ike Irish, might have the best hitting hands among college players in the draft. Undersized for a potential first baseman, but not lacking strength. Big hip/hand separation, hips open but don't compromise the outer third, back elbow collapses and hands find the baseball wherever it is. Can flatten his path to do oppo damage versus high heaters, or dip and rip to his pull side. Fairly complete hitter, changeups are his lone bugaboo. Has power. 110 mph EV90 this year, 17 bombs, strikeout rate dipping each season. Has played some third base in the past and looks awkward but not awful there, worth a shot in pro ball but is probably a first baseman. Isn't gonna be Pete Alonso or anything, but Yonder Alonso? Maybe.

A smaller-framed outfielder who takes monster hacks. Explosive rotator, plus-plus bat speed, but at his size, it takes Moss a ton of effort and elaborate mechanics to produce. Enormous movements, akin to a lefty Javier Báez. Has a hole in his swing up around his hands. Cuts stride with two strikes, fair contact performance with "round down" hit tool projection due to the high-effort nature of the swing. Has gotten some center field reps, but is a 4.45 runner and more likely a corner outfielder. Super fun, exciting mid-second round type of prospect.

Raw defender with exciting offensive tools. Projectable 6-foot-2 frame, feel for the barrel with natural loft. Hits from a deep crouch, tracks pitches well, low-ball power, oppo gap ability on pitches away. Likely second base fit puts a ton of pressure on the bat. Has barely faced average velocity, so there's risk here even though Mitchell's contact rate from travel ball play (84%) would indicate he's a stable prospect.

Compact infielder with big rotational athleticism. Swing has natural loft. Short to the baseball because of his size. Crushes fastballs and diagnoses breaking balls well; had a 2-to-1 ball-in-play-to-whiff ratio on the showcase circuit. Body is similar to Jett Williams and Kevin McGonigle when they came out - a compact guy whose perceived power ceiling is lower than his big-framed peers - but Melendez's skills and sneaky pop give him a shot to be an everyday middle infielder. Fits at shortstop on defense with plus actions and a nearly plus arm; range is closer to average. Has a better shot to play shortstop than all but a few players in the class, college or pro. Won't turn 18 until October, so will be juiced in models.

Ultra-twitchy, multi-positional athlete. Will run 4.15-ish to first. Has the speed to develop in center field, and the arm and athleticism to play shortstop. Smaller-framed guy with an amazing whole-body swing. Super aggressive leg kick and stride, hands have great rhythm despite how active they are before Southisene swings. Will occasionally turn on fastballs, but tends to spray hard contact all over the place. Posted a 78% contact rate combined in 2023 and 2024, was a little worse than that if you isolate 2024. Might end up as a superutility type due to elevated strikeouts, but has a rare combo of tools, athleticism, and a decent enough contact track record to be considered a late first rounder.

Multi-sport athlete (basketball) with monster ceiling and variance. Lanky outfielder with strong, explosive hands. Very likely to get much, much stronger as he fills out, and has a shot to develop plus-plus raw power. Lever length creates enormous hit tool risk; posted 67% contact rate in limited showcase play. Feel for center field is actually pretty good, but size may be a gating factor at maturity. If he goes to college and hits there, he'll go very high. Would play both basketball and baseball at Oklahoma if he goes to school.

Athletic freak with some of the most exciting long-term physical projection of any high school hitter in the class. Lanky 6-foot-5 frame with tons of room for strength. Among the class' standouts in athletic, strength, and mobility testing. Did not hit well on the showcase circuit. Swing was often out of sync and awkward looking, 72% contact rate with nearly as many whiffs as balls in play. Looks like he tracks pitches well, however, head stays on ball and can make mid-flight adjustment to breaking balls. Lever length creates long-term concern in this area. Goofy low ball power when he's on time and squares it. Bottom-hand dominant swing but still able to pull the ball on occasion. Huge finish behind him. Runs well enough to develop in center field. Extreme variance, similar to Alec Blair but probably more signable.

Big-framed, lefty-hitting catcher with a gorgeous swing but a scant showcase résumé. Raked at the World Wood Bat Championships in October, but was otherwise mostly absent from these kind of events and had to be tracked during varsity play instead. Has one of the best-looking swings in the draft and rare potential offensive output for a catcher. Athletic lower half, hands follow hips through contact, and which hand does the driving depends on pitch location (which is a rare skill). Oliveo can flatten his path to cover the top of the zone or dip into his lower body to scoop lower ones. There are times when it looks like he's doing a Juan Soto impressive. Obviously it's not that explosive, but it does look like Soto mechanically, so you can see why folks could be excited about Oliveto's bat. His defense is about as raw as a soon-to-be-pro catcher's defense could be. Wildly inaccurate arm due to messy footwork leaving his crouch, ball-blocking also looked rough last fall and will probably be worse handling pro stuff. These are the markers of a slower-developing player, but there's real enthusiasm around Oliveto's offensive potential.

Transferred from a Des Moines high school to IMG. Big power despite medium frame. One of the loudest and more consistent BPs of any 2025 high schooler. Put multiple balls in the Chase Field pool during PG All-American sessions. Head kicks around when he's swinging in games; ran a 70% contact rate on the showcase circuit, which isn't great. Swing has natural uppercut, but length into the hitting zone often causes him to be a little late and pepper the oppo gap. Swing-and-miss risk with lots of in-game whiffs versus pitches up and away from him. Power-over-hit corner profile, platoon look. Lots of lefty power means he's still a priority, second round type.

Crazy velo spike, went from touching 95 as a junior to touching 103 as a senior. Athletic build, three-quarters slot, doesn't throw with huge effort even though he's parked a 97-plus mph. Has some head violence but nothing crazy. Low-80s slider, velo delta might be detrimental in pro ball, but has 2,800-plus rpm. Fastball shape isn't great, but this is a mold-breaking prospect who might be the hardest-throwing high school pitcher of all time, though obviously the track record for guys throwing this hard this young isn't great.

Lafflam is an ultra-projectable high school righty with below-average control. All three of Lafflam's pitches have a shot to be real weapons, but he was often out of sync on the showcase circuit and struggled with walks. He has a cross-bodied delivery, and his arm often arrives late, with lots of arm-side misses with the fastball. Very loose and athletic for his size, it isn't shocking that Lafflam hasn't developed bodily sentience just yet, and it could take a while for it to arrive. He might have the biggest gap between his present and future fastball in the entire 2025 draft class. The fluidity with which Lafflam moves at his size, and the room he has for strength on his frame, suggest he could throw really, really hard one day. Both of his secondary pitches are nasty on occasion, but nowhere near the zone a lot of the time. If Lafflam either develops monster stuff or finds improved mechanical consistency, he'll end up being a decent big leaguer. If both happen, he'll be an impact starter.

Mid-80s slider with big glove-side length benefits the most from his polished feel. Changeups often sail on him. Size and pitchability foundation gives him a higher floor than most prep pitchers, fastball shape might cap his ceiling.

Low-to-the-ground infielder, fantastic bend, agility, and arm strength. Long, bottom-hand dominant swing that doesn't look especially functional in games but produces big power in BP. Glove-first hitting prospect, athletic dev project as a pitcher. Takes a massive cross-body stride down the mound, creating uphill angle with tail. Heater crept into the mid-90s last summer and has been more consistently there during the spring of 2025. Has too many arm-side misses right now with both his fastball and breaking stuff. Plus-flashing slider 78-82 mph, looks great when it actually turns the corner. Changeup is all over the place. Exciting raw athletic material on the mound with big hip/shoulder separation, lower body explosion, and natural north/south hand position coming out of a three quarters slot. A better prospect as a pitcher, but would be totally justifiable to draft Hammond as a hitter and spend most of his first 12 months in pro ball seeing just how viable the bat-to-ball skills are against pro stuff. He's going to be on an innings limit initially, anyway.

Athletic shortstop with impressive power. Muscular, but loose and mobile. Terrific low-to-the-ground defender, has the arm strength for shortstop but needs to polish accuracy. Strikeout issues plagued him on the showcase circuit, where he ran a 69% contact rate. Swing is loose and explosive but isn't always well-connected or well-timed. Bottom-hand dominant swing that works best when James can get extended. Thunderous power in his wrists and hands. Defensive fit at shortstop should allow room for elevated strikeouts as long as James is getting to power. Right tail outcome is akin to a Trevor Story type of offensive performance.

Two-year starter at UC San Diego, broke out on Cape Cod and with Team USA, transferred to LSU for his draft year. Posted 34% K% and 8% BB% in 108 IP as a junior. Will peak in the 94-97 mph range with his downhill fastball but more often live 92-94 with downhill plane and slightly below-average bat-missing performance. Breaking stuff is the real headliner here. Power mid-80s slider and upper-70s curveball, both of which benefit from the depth added by Eyanson's high arm slot. Throws strikes with all three offerings, so despite a stabby arm stroke in the back, has the repertoire and control to be developed as a starter in pro ball. Can create arm-side action on his breaking stuff to deal with lefties, slider included. Should be off the board in the early second round.

Russell spent his freshman season as a reliever - 0.89 ERA, 47 K, 7 BB, 30.1 IP - then had shoulder and elbow issues in 2024, which led to an internal brace UCL reconstruction. He was brought back at the start of the 2025 season, much more quickly than is typical for a TJ rehab, but then was shut down again for all of March. When he returned he worked once a week for two-ish inning s at a time through the end of the year, totalling 25 innings. Monster fastball potential. This is a 6-foot-6 guy with a sub-5-foot release height because his stride home is so low to the ground. His fastball averaged just shy of 94 mph in 2024 when Russell was healthy, and it has above-average vertical movement. Russell needs to find a second pitch. Slider was loose and hittable in limited usage in 2024, changeup took a huge step forward in 2025 even though it was his third-most used pitch. It's inconsistent, but the flashes of bat-missing action are there. Floor of a good fastball-heavy reliever, but given how little he's pitched, he might just be scratching the surface of mid-rotation starter potential.

Doesn't have huge top-end speed but did some incredible stuff on defense toward the end of the season, diving in the gaps with no regard for his own well being. Could be passable in center on grit and instincts, more likely to rove all over the outfield. Posted a 95% zone contact rate in 2025. Swings bent at the waist, which helps facilitate excellent plate coverage. Style can look slash-and-dash-y on the surface, but Teel has consistent feel for elevation. Makes well-struck contact to all fields. Would be a doubles machine if he had half a grade more power. Well-rounded fourth outfield prospect.

Grew up in Montreal then transferred to TNXL Academy in Florida for his senior spring. Ended up at Florida Gulf Coast for his freshman season, raked, then transferred to Arkansas and raked again. Slashed .346/.433/.561 with more walks than strikeouts in the SEC as a draft eligible soph. Incredibly skilled bat-to-ball prospect with ridiculous hand-eye coordination. Lets pitches travel deep before his swing ignites, makes well-struck contact to all fields. Geared for snatching pitches at the top of the zone, not as much for spoiling pitches below it. Smaller guy, on the fringe of what's typical for a big league hitter. Muscular 5-foot-9 guy. Below-average power, but not so little that it's a red flag. Four of his last six extra base hits were off of Liam Doyle, Kade Anderson, and Marcus Phillips. Uses the ground well to generate more power than one might expect from his little body. Played some second base at FGCU, a little bit of center field at Arkansas, but mostly left. Has the speed for center but ball skills aren't great; Arkansas moved him to a corner mid-season and left him there. Drafting club should try some combo of CF/2B just to see if he can do something that it's left field-only. Not quite Steven Kwan level feel for contact such that Davalan projects as a regular, but he does the most import thing (hit) and has proven it in the best conference.

Low-slot, cross-bodied southpaw with fastball hovering around 90 mph but playing up due to angle and command. Very similar look to Payton Tolle in terms of heater shape, angle and command, so it's ironic Uli is committed to TCU. Low-80s slider and changeup. Slidey plays up due to slot, changeup plays when located but tailed away from the zone often last summer. Softer build but big frame, reverse projection guy who could throw really hard on a good conditioning program.

Transferred from Utah Valley to LSU after two consecutive years with cartoonish stats for the Wolverines, then a .315/.458/.525 line as a junior. Twitchy, explosive, rare capacity for movement, body unfurls beautifully as he swings. Passed the test of hitting in a big conference with a 13.8% strikeout rate, but underlying power performance was underwhelming. MLB-average peak exit velo (110 mph), but hard-hit rate (38%) and EV90 (102) were closer to the college average. Can torch elevated fastballs to his pull side but is more of a pull-oriented singles hitter. Looked bigger and stronger in 2025, and it seemed to cost him some mobility on defense. Still has acrobatic body control and made some great throws across his body. Notes from shortstop defense at Utah Valley were not great, but Dickinson looks most comfortable throwing accurately while moving toward first base, so third base might be a second option for him. The simplicity in his hands keeps Dickinson on time and gives him a great chance to hit in pro ball, but lack of impact contact might relegate him to second-division status at second if he can't play somewhere else.

Showed steady improvement as a hitter at Michigan with huge reduction in strikeouts (from 22% down to 13%) as a junior. Was a two-way player for his first two seasons, up to 93 on the mound. Arm strength and speed might allow for him to branch out on defense in pro ball. Hands aren't great at second base, but his actions around the bag are. Tough kid, stands in there and will take a baserunner in his lap as he's completing the turn. Offense might be short for second base if it turns out to be the only position he can play. Authoritative hands but swing is relatively grooved. Might have vulnerability to elevated heaters in pro ball. Makes consistently hard contact, but lacks high-end raw power. Contact and peak power data were roughly average for a college hitter. Looks more like a potential second-division second baseman barring a move up he defensive spectrum to shortstop or center field in pro ball. Probably needs to try a couple other positions anyway to facilitate a utility role.

Draft-eligible sophomore who hit .285/.386/.502 as freshman shortstop and entered 2025 as a potential top 15 pick. Really struggled on defense and ended up roving all over the infield, finishing the season at second base. Might not be an infielder at all, had issues with routine plays. Hit .315/.435/.531 with nearly as many walks as strikeouts in 2025 but has some scary mechanical and batted ball markers. Swing triggers late and is quite long, leading Curley to pepper the opposite field. Might have issues with tardiness versus pro fastballs. Strapping 6-foot-3 guy with strength and verve in his wrists, so he's capable of hitting for oppo power even when he's late. Passive hitter with 34% swing rate and 60% swing rate when the pitch is right down the middle. Speaks to some artificiality regarding his plate discipline. Power-hitting bounce-back candidate whose stock fell as much as anyone for on-field reasons in 2025.

High-ceiling'd, high-variance lefty-hitting infielder with big time frame projection. Explosive hitting hands, broad-shouldered 6-foot-3 frame with loads of room for strength. Really exciting at first glance, but ultimately K'd quite a bit on the showcase circuit and has considerable hit tool risk. Potential for big power could make a likely below-average contact profile workable, especially if Franco can stay at shortstop. Size and mobility looked like more of third base fit last summer. Removed his name from the draft a few days prior to selection and is headed to TCU.

Fundamentally sound shortstop defender with soft, sure hands and enough arm. Among the lower-variance high school prospects with realistic utility ceiling.

Two-year starter at East Carolina before transfer to Arkansas. Command-oriented pitchability lefty with four pitches. Funky, short-striding, low-slot delivery. Physically mature. Deep pitch mix. Fastball was up to 97 late in the season but sat about 92 all year and generated well-below-average swing-and-miss. Secondary stuff is driving Root's profile. Plus low-80s curveball, tailing-mid-80s changeup, upper-80s cutter. All are commanded well enough for them to play like above-average pitches, and for Root to work efficiently as a starter. Will probably be one of the quicker movers from this draft class, a high-probability backend starter.

A 6-foot-7 lankster, projectable frame, threw strikes for three years as a starter at Michigan State. Not a ton of effort in the delivery, short-strider with some low slot crossfire, all upper body. Fastball 90-93 with tailing life up in zone. Paired with an above-average low 80s changeup, which has late fade and drop and consistent arm side location; plus miss and chase combo. Below-average upper-70s slider, not much power to it, lives toward the top of the zone more like a slow motion cutter. A breaking ball with more finish and an actual cutter would allow Dzierwa to have a big league backend starter's mix.
